D O N E I S N O T T H E
DESTINATION

Over the years, we have strengthened our platform, expanded our 
capabilities, deepened client relationships, and built a diversified and 
integrated wealth management franchise. Each step has made us stronger. 
Yet, each step has also revealed a larger opportunity ahead. 
Nowhere is this truer than in India. As wealth creation accelerates, 
financialisation deepens, and millions of investors enter the formal 
financial ecosystem, the opportunity before the industry is significantly 
larger than what has been realised so far. The horizon continues to expand. 
This is why we do not view progress as a destination. We view it as a 
responsibility.
A responsibility to serve clients better. To build stronger capabilities. 
To innovate faster. To create greater value for all our stakeholders.
The work that brought us here matters. But it is the work ahead that 
excites us even more.
Because every milestone reached becomes a new starting line. 
For us, done is not the destination. It is where the next chapter begins.
Success has a way of creating a false sense of completion.
A target is achieved. A milestone is crossed. A business 
is scaled. It is tempting to pause and believe the journey 
has reached its destination.
But the most meaningful journeys rarely work that way. 
At Nuvama, every achievement has taught us the 
same lesson: Progress does not end at a milestone. 
It begins there.

Our strength lies in the seamless integration of Wealth Management, Asset Management, Asset Services, and Capital 
Markets, operating as one unified platform. Each business brings deep domain expertise and distinct capabilities, 
enabling us to deliver comprehensive, tailored solutions while leveraging the scale and synergies of the broader 
Nuvama ecosystem.
For our clients, this integrated model provides access to a full spectrum of financial solutions – from bespoke wealth 
solutions and estate planning, institutional-quality investment strategies, and efficient custody and reporting services, 
to capital markets expertise that supports entrepreneurial and corporate ambitions. Through a single trusted partner, 
clients can address their evolving financial needs across the wealth lifecycle.
For Nuvama, this interconnected platform enhances cross-functional collaboration, deepens client relationships, 
drives operating leverage, and fosters innovation. The result is a differentiated ecosystem that delivers greater value to 
clients, strengthens our competitive positioning, and exemplifies the philosophy of One Nuvama.

Stronger Today.
Ready for Tomorrow.
M E S S AG E F R O M T H E C H A I R P E R S O N
D E A R S H A R E H O L D E R S ,
This was another year of sustained progress for 
our organisation. We continued to strengthen 
our client proposition, enhance enterprise 
capabilities and invest in the foundations that 
will support future growth. Importantly, the 
year reinforced the strength of our diversified 
yet integrated business model, where wealth 
management, asset management, asset 
services and capital markets capabilities 
work together to create a differentiated and 
resilient platform. Alongside business growth, 
we remained focussed on strengthening our 
people, technology, governance and institutional 
capabilities, recognising that enduring 
institutions must continually evolve to create 
long-term value for stakeholders.
A World in Transition
FY 2025-26 was marked by significant 
developments across trade, technology and 
geopolitics.
The resurgence of trade protectionism, evolving 
tariff frameworks and geopolitical tensions 
contributed to a more fragmented global 
landscape. Supply chains remained vulnerable 
to geopolitical disruptions, while markets 
periodically grappled with uncertainty around 
inflation, growth and policy direction. At the 
same time, artificial intelligence moved rapidly 
from experimentation to application, beginning 
to reshape industries and business models at an 
unprecedented pace. Despite these challenges, 
the global economy demonstrated notable 
resilience, supported by continued innovation 
and investment.
India remained relatively well positioned 
amidst this backdrop. Supported by proactive 
monetary and fiscal measures, ongoing reforms 
and a resilient domestic economy, India 
continued to be among the fastest-growing 
major economies globally. Yet the year was not 
without challenges. Corporate earnings grew at 
a moderate pace across certain sectors, capital 
flows remained volatile at times, and equity 
markets experienced periods of correction and 
uncertainty as investors responded to shifting 
global developments.
Encouragingly, India’s structural growth drivers 
remain firmly intact. Rising formalisation, 
digital adoption, infrastructure investments, 
growing entrepreneurial activity and increasing 
participation in financial markets continue to 
strengthen the country’s long-term growth 
trajectory. Despite near-term uncertainties, India’s 
economic fundamentals continue to provide a 
strong foundation for long-term wealth creation.
The Next Chapter of Wealth 
Management
The wealth management industry is entering a 
new phase of evolution.
Globally, wealth continues to grow, but the 
industry is being reshaped by powerful structural 
shifts. Artificial intelligence is transforming 
advisory models and operating economics, inter-
generational wealth transfer is redefining client 
needs, and investors are increasingly seeking 
holistic solutions rather than standalone products. 
At the same time, independent wealth managers 
are emerging as a formidable force. According 
to the Boston Consulting Group Global Wealth 
Report, they now manage roughly a quarter of 
high-net-worth assets in the United States, hold 
meaningful market share in established centres 
such as Switzerland and Germany, and are among 
the fastest-growing channels in markets including 
the UAE, Singapore and India.
Against this backdrop, India stands out as one 
of the most compelling wealth management 
opportunities globally. Emerging markets are 
expected to add nearly USD 7 Tn of financial 
wealth by 2030, with India contributing more 
than USD 2 Tn (by clients with wealth above 
USD 2,50,000) – the largest share among 
emerging economies.
The opportunity is being powered by rising 
affluence, increasing financialisation of savings, 
greater participation in capital markets, growing 
adoption of alternative investments and a rising 
preference for professional advice. Wealth 
creation is also becoming more broad-based, 
extending beyond traditional metropolitan 
centres, and deepening across segments.
It is my pleasure to present 
the Annual Report of Nuvama 
Wealth Management Limited 
for FY 2025-26. On behalf of the 
Board, I would like to thank our 
clients, employees, partners, 
regulators and shareholders 
for their continued trust 
and support. In a year 
characterised by heightened 
global uncertainty, evolving 
market dynamics and rapid 
technological changes, Nuvama 
continued to demonstrate 
resilience, adaptability and 
steadfast commitment to 
long-term value creation.
Supported by proactive 
monetary and fiscal 
measures, ongoing reforms 
and a resilient domestic 
economy, India continued to 
be among the fastest-growing 
major economies globally.

As the market expands, however, so does 
competition. Banks - both public and private 
sector, wealth managers, independent 
advisors, and digital platforms are increasingly 
converging towards similar client segments. In 
this environment, differentiation is shifting from 
product access to the quality of advice, strength 
of relationships, depth of solutions, technology 
enablement and the ability to consistently deliver 
client outcomes.
We believe the next phase of industry leadership 
will belong to institutions that combine advice, 
solutions, technology and trust within an 
integrated, client-centric model.
Building Nuvama for What Comes 
Next
At Nuvama, we continue to build with a long-term 
perspective. Our strategic focus remains anchored 
around three interconnected pillars: People, 
Platform and Solutions.
People remain at the heart of our organisation. 
During FY 2025-26, our employee strength 
exceeded 3,400 professionals, reflecting a 7% 
CAGR over the last five years. Our relationship 
manager franchise remained strong at 
approximately 1,250 professionals despite 
heightened competitive intensity across the 
industry. We continued to invest in leadership 
development, capability building and fostering a 
culture that encourages learning, innovation and 
excellence.
Platform continues to be a key differentiator. 
We remained focussed on building institutional-
grade technology infrastructure underpinned by 
resilience, security and scalability. During the year, 
we modernised 60% of our application landscape 
and further expanded our technology footprint 
across datacentres, exchange colocation 
infrastructure and cloud environments. 
Our platforms continued to earn industry 
recognition while maintaining high standards 
of governance and security.
Equally important, we advanced our AI 
journey from experimentation to capability. 
AI is now being embedded across advisory, 
operations, client servicing, risk management 
and decision-support workflows. We 
believe AI will be a defining force in wealth 
management, reshaping both client 
experience and operating models, and are 
investing thoughtfully to harness its potential 
responsibly and at scale.
Solutions remain central to our client-first 
philosophy. During the year, we sharpened our 
wealth management proposition, expanded 
product capabilities within asset management, 
strengthened offerings within asset services 
and deepened coverage across institutional 
equities and investment banking. Together, 
these investments further enhanced our 
ability to deliver comprehensive advice and 
integrated solutions to clients.
The progress made across these pillars 
has been recognised through several 
industry accolades and independent 
awards, reinforcing our belief that sustained 
investment in people, platforms and solutions 
creates enduring competitive advantage.
Trust, Governance and 
Responsible Growth
Trust remains the foundation of every 
successful financial institution.
As our business continues to evolve, 
governance remains a strategic priority. During 
the year, we further strengthened governance 
frameworks across the organisation and 
enhanced Board oversight across key entities. 
We also onboarded experienced Independent 
Directors across our asset management and 
mutual fund trustee entities, bringing diverse 
perspectives and deep institutional expertise.
We continued to strengthen risk management 
capabilities through greater automation, 
enhanced surveillance and improved control 
frameworks. Focus areas included insider 
trading safeguards, regulatory compliance 
and preparedness for emerging frameworks 
relating to data protection and privacy.
We believe governance must evolve alongside the 
business and the environment in which it operates. More 
than a compliance obligation, it is a strategic capability 
that strengthens trust, protects stakeholders, creates 
competitive advantage and enables sustainable growth.
Recognising the growing importance of cyber 
resilience and responsible technology adoption, 
we conducted comprehensive cybersecurity 
assessments and further strengthened our 
information security architecture. The Board 
and senior leadership team also participated 
in focussed learning initiatives covering AI, ESG 
and other emerging areas shaping the future of 
financial services.
We believe governance must evolve alongside the 
business and the environment in which it operates. 
More than a compliance obligation, it is a strategic 
capability that strengthens trust, protects 
stakeholders, creates competitive advantage and 
enables sustainable growth.
People, Purpose and Sustainability
At Nuvama, we believe sustainable value creation 
extends beyond financial performance.
Our people remain the foundation of our growth 
and success. During the year, we continued to 
invest in leadership development, capability 
building, employee wellbeing and fostering a 
culture of learning, collaboration and continuous 
improvement. As the organisation scales, 
preserving our values and entrepreneurial spirit 
remains a key priority.
Beyond our organisation, we remain committed 
to creating a positive impact for the communities 
we serve through Corporate Social Responsibility 
(CSR) initiatives focussed on education, skill 
development and environmental sustainability. 
We also continued to strengthen ESG governance 
through active Board oversight, robust policies and 
responsible business practices.
These efforts reflect our belief that enduring 
success is built not only on financial outcomes, 
but also on the positive impact we create for our 
people, communities and society at large.
Looking Ahead with Confidence
The future will undoubtedly present challenges. 
Competitive intensity will continue to increase. 
Client expectations will evolve. Regulatory

We believe Nuvama is well positioned for this

As we move forward with renewed vigour and

While we take pride, with gratitude and humility, in

of our responsibilities and are of the firm belief 
that our growth journey will continue without a

‘The woods are lovely, dark and deep,

Building Beyond  
Milestones
M E S S AG E F R O M T H E M D & C E O
FY 2025-26 was a year of meaningful progress 
across our businesses and our institution. 
Every milestone achieved has strengthened 
our conviction that the opportunities before us 
across wealth management, asset management, 
asset services and capital markets are 
significantly larger than the outcomes we 
celebrate today.
For us, Done is not the destination. It is a 
reminder that progress creates responsibility. 
The responsibility to serve our clients better, 
build stronger capabilities, raise our standards 
further and prepare for opportunities that are 
only beginning to emerge.
Delivering Another Year of Strong 
Performance
The year unfolded against a backdrop of tariff-
led uncertainty, changing regulatory dynamics, 
geopolitical developments, evolving market 
conditions and intensifying competition. While 
these factors periodically influenced investor 
sentiment and market direction, they also 
reinforced the importance of trusted advice, 
strong execution and resilient business models.
Against this backdrop, Nuvama delivered 
another year of strong and balanced growth. 
Revenue for FY 2025-26 stood at ` 3,122 
crore, while operating profit after tax reached 
` 1,049 crore. Return on equity continued to be 
strong at 28.1%. Client assets across our platform 
surpassed ` 4.5 lakh crore, reflecting the trust 
that clients continue to place in our franchise. 
Importantly, our diversified business model once 
again demonstrated its strength, with every 
major business delivering healthy multi-year 
profit growth. These outcomes were the result 
of disciplined execution, a client-first approach 
and the dedication of our teams across the 
organisation.
Deepening Client Relationships 
Across Businesses
Our purpose has always been anchored 
around doing it right - building enduring client 
relationships rather than pursuing short-
term outcomes. We believe that when clients 
entrust us with an increasingly larger part of

Mr. Birendra Kumar is an Independent Director and Chairperson of the Company and an

Economy Overview
Global Economy: A Year of Tariffs, Technology 
and Tensions
FY 2026 was a defining year from a global economic 
perspective, shaped by significant developments across 
three critical fronts - trade, technology and geopolitics. 
The year began with a sharp escalation in trade policy, 
following the US announcement of ‘Liberation Day’ 
tariffs on April 2, 2025. This was followed by a period of 
heightened uncertainty, with tariff rates for some trading 
partners rising as high as 50%. Although the US Supreme 
Court struck down select tariffs, offering partial relief, 
the overall effective US tariff rate remained elevated at 
around 10%, levels not seen since the post-World War II 
era, signalling the end of the prolonged phase of low global 
tariffs.
Alongside this, FY 2026 witnessed a step-change in 
technological disruption, led by rapid advancements in 
AI. Major AI firms such as Anthropic, Google, Meta and 
others accelerated the development of enterprise-
grade AI models, infrastructure and applications, pushing 
adoption into more critical use cases. This supported a 
sharp rise in AI-linked investment and created second-
order effects across global supply chains, driving demand 
for semiconductors, data centres and power capacity, 
while also raising concerns around labour displacement, 
particularly in services.
Geopolitical tensions further intensified during the year, 
culminating in a direct confrontation involving the US, 
Iran and Israel. The conflict led to the closure of the Strait 
of Hormuz, disrupting global supply chains and driving 
a sharp increase in crude oil prices and shipping costs, 
which heightened global volatility and further complicated 
the inflation outlook.
Despite overlapping shocks, the global economy remained 
relatively resilient in CY 2026, with world GDP growth 
projected at 3.1%, moderating from around 3.4% in CY 
2025, according to the International Monetary Fund’s 
World Economic Outlook, April 2026. However, growth 
trends remained uneven across regions. The US economy 
improved modestly to 2.3% in CY 2026 from 2.1% in CY 
2025, while China’s growth moderated to 4.4% from 5.0% 
and the Euro Area slowed to 1.1% from 1.4%.
Looking ahead, renewed tensions and intermittent 
escalations continue to create uncertainty around trade 
flows, energy markets and supply chains, with limited 
visibility on when conditions may fully normalise. While 
supply-side constraints could gradually unwind over 
time and the benefits of AI adoption are expected to 
increasingly translate into productivity gains, supporting 
medium-term growth, risks remain elevated. Any 
prolonged geopolitical disruptions or supply shocks could 
spill over into broader demand weakness globally. In this 
environment, policy responses, structural reforms and 
balance sheet resilience will play a critical role in shaping 
the trajectory of global growth.
India: Anchoring Growth through Policy Support
In a year marked by global uncertainty, India stood out as 
a policy oasis, supported by coordinated monetary, fiscal 
and regulatory measures aimed at sustaining growth. 
Under the new RBI governor, monetary policy turned 
decisively accommodative, with cumulative repo rate 
cuts of 125 bps bringing the policy rate down to 5.25%, 
alongside liquidity support and regulatory easing. This 
was complemented by fiscal and tax measures focussed 
on consumption and ease of living, including relief in 
individual income-tax rates, GST rate rationalisation 
through simplified slabs and lower rates on several goods 
and services, as well as the removal of GST on individual 
life and health insurance premiums.
These measures gradually translated into improved 
domestic activity, with bank credit growth strengthening 
during the year and reaching 14.1% YoY by end-March 
2026, compared with 11.1% a year earlier, according to RBI 
data. High-frequency indicators, including automobile 
sales and other consumption-linked activity, also pointed 
to a gradual revival in underlying momentum. However, 
the recovery remained uneven, with corporate earnings 
staying under pressure across several sectors amid 
subdued demand conditions and global uncertainty.
Given the challenging external environment, geopolitical 
tensions and elevated tariffs weighed on India’s goods 
exports, which grew modestly by around 1% in FY 2026. 
Services exports remained resilient, rising by nearly 9% 
in USD terms, helping cushion the impact of subdued 
merchandise trade. However, global risk aversion, volatile 
capital markets and relatively attractive opportunities 
across other emerging markets contributed to foreign 
portfolio investor outflows and weaker capital inflows 
into India. Despite these headwinds, India remained 
among the fastest-growing major economies, with real 
GDP growth rising to 7.7% in FY 2026 from 7.1% in FY 2025, 
according to MoSPI’s Provisional Estimates released on 
June 5, 2026. Inflation dynamics were also favourable, 
with headline CPI easing from 4.6% in FY 2025 to around 
4.0% in FY 2026, supported by softer food inflation. On 
the external policy front, India continued to strengthen 
trade linkages, including the India–UK trade agreement 
and ongoing engagement with the US and other key 
partners, supporting export competitiveness and supply 
chain diversification.
Looking ahead, while INR depreciation could enhance 
India’s export competitiveness, it may also raise import 
costs, particularly for crude oil and other key inputs, 
thereby adding to inflationary pressures and weighing on 
the broader macroeconomic outlook. Domestic liquidity 
conditions are also expected to remain comfortable, 
supported by the RBI’s continued liquidity measures, 
which is also reflected from the fact that liquidity has 
remained in surplus despite pressure on India’s BoP, which 
is a historic anomaly.
Overall, India’s macroeconomic resilience remains 
underpinned by a strong corporate balance sheet, a 
credible policy framework, ongoing structural reforms, 
rising formalisation, rapid digitalisation, and sustained 
investments in infrastructure and manufacturing are likely 
to anchor long-term growth. In an increasingly fragmented 
global economy, India continues to strengthen its position 
as a key driver of global growth.
Industry Overview and Outlook
India’s long-term growth story is being shaped by a 
powerful convergence of structural forces that extend 
well beyond cyclical economic trends. Strong economic 
growth, rising disposable incomes, increasing formalisation, 
digital adoption and progressive regulatory advancements 
are reshaping how capital is created, allocated and 
compounded across the economy. At the same time, a 
high domestic savings base, accelerating financialisation 
of household wealth and growing participation of 
domestic investors in capital markets are strengthening 
the foundations of sustainable growth.
These structural tailwinds are expected to drive a 
significant expansion in wealth creation over the coming 
decade. As per BCG’s Global Wealth Report 2026, India 
is expected to add over USD 2 Tn in financial wealth by 
2030, growing at a 12% CAGR (Affluent and emerging HNW 
segment with investable assets above USD 250,000). This 
growth is supported by deeper financial inclusion, rising 
investor participation and an increasingly mature financial 
ecosystem, keeping India among the most compelling 
long-term wealth opportunities globally.

2. High Domestic Savings Supporting Long-
Term Capital Formation
India’s consistently high savings rate reflects one of the 
country’s most important structural strengths – a large 
and growing pool of domestic capital. As per World Bank, 
Gross domestic savings increased from 13% of GDP in 1975 
to a peak of 37% in 2007 and currently stand at around 
30%, comfortably above the global average of 26.2%. This 
strong savings culture provides a durable foundation for 
capital formation and long-term economic growth.

3. Financialisation of Household Savings
India’s household savings landscape is undergoing a 
gradual but meaningful transformation, with savings 
increasingly moving beyond traditional physical assets 
such as real estate and gold towards financial assets. 
Rising incomes, greater financial awareness, wider product 
availability and improved digital access are encouraging 
greater participation in mutual funds, insurance, pension 
products and other market-linked investment avenues.
Despite this progress, India continues to have one of the 
lowest shares of financial assets in overall household 
wealth relative to many major economies, where financial 
assets account for 25.8% of the total gross savings. 
This gap highlights the substantial headroom for further 
financialisation as incomes rise, financial literacy improves 
and capital market participation deepens. At the same 
time, product innovation is broadening the investible 
universe by converting traditionally illiquid or physical 
assets into accessible, regulated and market-linked 
instruments. REITs and InvITs are enabling investors 
to participate in income-generating real estate and 
infrastructure assets, while ETFs are providing low-cost, 
transparent exposure to asset classes such as gold 
and equities. This evolution is helping deepen financial 
markets, improve diversification and create new avenues 
for household savings to participate in India’s long-term 
growth story.

4. Digital India Transforming Access, Inclusion 
and Efficiency
Over the past decade, India’s digital transformation has 
reshaped how citizens access services, transact, learn 
and participate in the economy. Supported by one of the 
world’s largest Digital Public Infrastructure ecosystems, 
initiatives such as Aadhaar, UPI, DigiLocker and the JAM 
trinity (Jan Dhan Accounts, Aadhaar and Mobile) have 
significantly enhanced financial inclusion, reduced friction 
in service delivery, and improved transparency across 
the economy. As per The Digital India report by PIB, as of 
March 2026, over 109 crore people had internet access, 
broadband subscribers exceeded 106 crore, and UPI 
processed more than 24,000 crore transactions during 
FY 2026, underscoring the scale of digital adoption across 
both urban and rural India.
Beyond improving productivity and reducing transaction 
costs, Digital India is fostering financial inclusion, 
broadening access to investment and banking services, 
and creating a more connected and efficient economic 
ecosystem. As digital adoption continues to deepen, it 
is expected to remain a key enabler of economic growth, 
financialisation and wealth creation.
5. Robust Regulatory Oversight Strengthening 
Market Confidence
India’s financial services industry is entering a more 
mature phase, with rising participation across mutual 
funds, alternatives, capital markets, insurance, lending and 
wealth solutions.
As the ecosystem becomes larger, more digital and 
increasingly interconnected, regulatory oversight has 
also evolved, with institutions such as SEBI, RBI, IRDAI and 
AMFI playing an important role in strengthening market 
conduct, risk management, transparency and investor 
protection standards.
Recent regulatory actions have covered a broad set of 
areas, including tighter oversight of derivatives trading, 
enhanced margin and collateral frameworks, greater 
transparency in AIFs and PMS, sharper disclosure 
requirements for listed companies and intermediaries, 
and stronger governance expectations across market 
participants. SEBI’s continued focus on retail investor 
protection, particularly in the equity derivatives segment, 
reflects the need to balance rapid market deepening with 
orderly and sustainable participation.
Beyond securities markets, regulatory tightening has also 
been visible across banking and insurance. RBI’s evolving 
prudential framework for project finance, liquidity and 
funding norms is aimed at strengthening balance-
sheet resilience and harmonising risk standards across 
regulated entities. Similarly, IRDAI’s consolidated insurance 
regulations, including sharper product governance, 
surrender-value disclosures and the development of 
digital market infrastructure such as Bima Sugam, are 
intended to improve customer outcomes and expand 
insurance penetration.
For the industry, this environment raises compliance 
expectations and near-term adaptation costs, but it 
also creates a stronger foundation for long-term growth. 
Well-governed and well-capitalised platforms are likely 
to benefit as regulatory intensity favours transparency, 
institutionalisation and scale. Over time, a robust 
regulatory architecture should deepen trust, improve

6. Demographic Dividend and Intergenerational 
Wealth Transfer
India’s wealth management opportunity is being 
structurally reshaped by two powerful long-term forces: 
a young, aspirational population entering its prime 
earning years and a large intergenerational transfer 
of wealth. Together, these trends are expected to 
expand household wealth creation, deepen demand for 
professional advice and create a broader opportunity 
set for integrated wealth management platforms. 
India’s demographic dividend represents a unique 
opportunity to support long-term economic growth and 
expand household wealth creation.
According to the United Nations World Population 
Prospects 2024, India is home to about 1.46 billion 
people in 2025, with nearly 68% of the population in the 
working-age group of 15–64 years and a median age of 
approximately 29 years, making it one of the youngest 
major economies globally. As this large working-age 
cohort enters higher income and savings phases, it is 
expected to create a sizeable opportunity for wealth 
managers by increasing the need for financial planning, 
investment advisory and long-term wealth solutions. 
  
At the same time, India is entering a phase of significant 
wealth succession and family wealth formalisation. Reports 
indicate that around USD 1.3-1.5 Tn of wealth may transfer 
to the next generation over the next decade, while the 
number of Indian family offices has expanded sharply from 
around 45 in 2018 to nearly 300 by 2024. This creates a 
strong demand for integrated platforms that can support 
succession planning, portfolio diversification, governance, 
estate planning, alternatives, philanthropy, and global 
allocation.

2. Accelerating Shift Towards Capital Market 
Led Investment Solutions
Investor preferences continue to evolve from traditional 
transaction-based investing towards professionally 
managed and advisory-led solutions. Sustained domestic 
capital market participation, increasing financial literacy, 
and the growing complexity of investment decisions have 
accelerated demand for managed products across wealth 
segments.
PMS, AIF, mutual funds, structured products, and 
discretionary portfolio solutions continue to gain 
market share as investors seek professional expertise, 
diversification, and risk-adjusted returns. This structural 
shift is also supporting the industry’s transition from 
distribution-led models towards recurring fee-based 
advisory relationships, resulting in stronger client 
engagement and more predictable revenue streams for 
wealth managers.
3. Offshore Investing Emerging as a Key Wealth 
Management Theme
Global diversification is increasingly becoming an 
important portfolio consideration for Indian HNIs and 
UHNIs, driven by the need to access a broader opportunity 
set, diversify geographic and currency exposure, and 
participate in global investment themes. As client wealth 
grows and investment sophistication increases, demand 
for offshore investment solutions continues to gain 
momentum.
This trend is enabled through established regulatory 
channels, such as the Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS) 
for individuals and the Overseas Direct Investment (ODI) 
framework for entities, which allow structured, compliant 
access to international markets and offshore investment 
structures. These routes are increasingly used by HNIs, 
UHNIs, and family offices for global portfolio allocation, 
alternative investments, and overseas structuring.
The development of GIFT City and the International 
Financial Services Centre (IFSC) ecosystem has further 
strengthened India’s offshore wealth management 
infrastructure by providing a regulated platform for 
accessing global investment opportunities. Wealth 
managers are increasingly leveraging strategic partnerships 
with External Asset Managers (EAMs), international 
product providers, and global investment platforms 
to offer clients access to international equities, global 
fixed income, alternative investments, and discretionary 
portfolio solutions.

creation through entrepreneurship, capital markets, and 
business ownership has resulted in greater demand for 
holistic financial planning, estate structuring, governance 
frameworks, tax optimisation, and succession planning.

Technology continues to reshape the wealth management 
value chain, enhancing efficiency, scalability, and client 
engagement. Digital onboarding, portfolio analytics, client 
reporting, and integrated advisory platforms have become 
key differentiators across the industry.
The adoption of artificial intelligence is further 
accelerating this transformation through personalised 
investment recommendations, predictive analytics, 
portfolio monitoring, risk assessment, and enhanced client 
servicing capabilities. AI-driven solutions are enabling 
wealth managers to deliver more customised experiences 
while improving operational productivity and decision-
making processes.
7. Rising Investor Interests across Wealth 
Management Landscape
The competitive landscape continues to evolve with 
participation from private banks, standalone wealth 
managers, boutique advisory firms, asset managers, 
fintech platforms, and global financial institutions seeking 
to expand their presence in India. The sector has witnessed 
the entry of several new wealth management platforms 
and advisory firms, attracted by strong industry growth 
prospects.
The industry has also seen heightened interest from 
private equity investors, with significant capital being 
deployed into wealth management businesses to support 
platform expansion, technology investments, acquisitions, 
and talent acquisition. This influx of capital has further 
intensified competition and accelerated industry 
consolidation.
At the same time, relationship managers (RMs) remain a 
critical differentiator in client acquisition and retention, 
specially in the UHNI and HNI segment. Growing demand 
for experienced advisory talent has led to increased 
competition for high-performing RMs, resulting in higher 
compensation costs and elevated attrition levels across 
the industry. As competition shifts beyond product 
offerings toward advisory quality, client experience, and 
relationship depth, firms are increasingly focussed on 
strengthening talent retention, technology capabilities, 
and differentiated service models to sustain growth and 
market share.
Asset Management
The asset management industry continues to demonstrate structural resilience, supported by rising financial savings, 
deeper investor participation, expanding distribution networks, and increasing acceptance of professionally managed 
investment products. Investors are increasingly looking for diversified, transparent and risk-calibrated investment 
solutions across traditional and alternative asset classes.

Assets Classes
India’s alternatives industry is witnessing a steady 
increase in domestic capital participation, driven by 
growing allocations from family offices, HNIs, UHNIs, 
banks and government-linked institutions. Rising 
wealth creation, greater awareness of private market 
opportunities and the search for differentiated returns 
are supporting this transition.
A significant opportunity remains in expanding participation 
from domestic institutional investors, including pension 
funds, retirement funds, insurance companies and banks. 
Reflecting this trend, the share of domestic investors in 
funds raised across Category I and II AIFs increased from 
50.3% in March 2024 to 52.7% in June 2025, resulting in 
incremental fund inflows of approximately ₹72,667 crore. 
Greater domestic participation has the potential to further 
deepen the alternatives ecosystem and support long-
term capital formation for entrepreneurship, innovation 
and infrastructure development.
1. Mutual Funds
The mutual fund industry remains a key beneficiary of 
India's increasing financialisation, supported by rising retail 
participation, growing investor awareness and sustained 
SIP inflows. Industry AUM increased to ₹73.7 lakh crore as 
of March 2026, registering 12.2% YoY growth, while annual 
SIP contributions reached a record ₹3.49 lakh crore. The 
industry also witnessed broad-based participation across 
investor segments and geographies, with B-30 cities 
accounting for nearly 18-20% of industry AUM, reflecting 
deeper penetration beyond metropolitan markets.
Mutual funds continue to benefit from their accessibility, 
regulatory oversight, product diversity and suitability for 
long-term wealth creation. The launch of lifecycle funds 
further expands the product suite by offering goal-based, 
age-aligned allocation solutions for investors across life 
stages. As investor participation broadens and financial 
savings continue to migrate towards market-linked 
products, the industry remains well positioned to capture 
a growing share of household wealth.

Evolving Investment Vehicles across Risk-Return Spectrum
2. Specialised Investment Funds 
The introduction of Specialised Investment Funds (SIFs) 
marks a significant product innovation within the asset 
management landscape. Positioned between traditional 
mutual funds and higher-ticket solutions such as PMS 
and AIFs, SIFs provide eligible investors access to more 
sophisticated and strategy-led investment approaches 
within a regulated asset management framework.
Investor adoption has been encouraging, with SIF AUM 
crossing ₹23,000 crore as of July 2026. Hybrid-oriented 
strategies accounted for 71% of total SIF assets, while 
equity-oriented strategies represented the remaining 
29%. The emergence of SIFs reflects growing demand 
from affluent investors for differentiated, outcome-
oriented and risk-adjusted investment solutions, further 
expanding the industry's product spectrum and growth 
opportunities.

3. Alternates
The alternatives segment has emerged as one of the 
fastest-growing areas of India's asset management 
industry, driven by increasing investor sophistication, 
rising allocations from HNIs, UHNIs and family offices, and 
growing demand for diversification beyond traditional 
asset classes. Investors are increasingly allocating 
capital across both listed and private market alternative 
strategies in pursuit of differentiated return streams, 
portfolio diversification and access to unique investment 
opportunities.
a) Listed Alternatives – PMS and Category III AIFs
The listed alternatives segment, comprising Portfolio 
Management Services (PMS) and Category III AIFs, 
continues to witness strong growth as investors seek more 
customised, concentrated and alpha-oriented investment 
strategies. PMS solutions are increasingly preferred by 
affluent investors for their flexibility, portfolio customisation 
and ability to deliver differentiated investment outcomes. 
As of April 2026, the PMS industry managed over ₹42 lakh 
crore in AUM across more than 2.1 lakh investor accounts, 
reflecting growing investor sophistication and increased 
adoption of professionally managed portfolios.

Category III AIFs have also gained traction, supported 
by increasing acceptance of long-short, market-neutral 
and other hedge-fund-like strategies. These vehicles 
provide investors with access to sophisticated listed-
market strategies that go beyond traditional long-only 
approaches, while benefiting from a regulated investment 
framework. Together, PMS and Category III AIFs are 
expanding the spectrum of listed-market investment 
opportunities and driving the evolution of India's managed 
investments landscape.
Further, the establishment of Association of Portfolio 
Managers in India (APMI) by SEBI represents an important 
milestone for India’s PMS industry, aimed at promoting 
industry-wide standardisation, strengthening governance 
and compliance frameworks, enhancing investor 
protection, and fostering greater transparency. This is 
expected to further institutionalise the PMS ecosystem 
and support its long-term growth.
b) Private Markets – Private Equity, Private Credit, 
Real Assets (Infrastructure, Real Estate) and 
Venture Debt
Private markets have become an increasingly important 
component of investor portfolios, with rising allocations 
towards private equity, private credit, venture debt, 
commercial real estate, infrastructure and other private 
market strategies. Investors are increasingly seeking 
exposure to long-term growth opportunities, alternative 
sources of yield and returns that are less correlated with 
public market cycles.
The AIF industry has been the primary vehicle driving 
participation in private markets. AIF commitments 
increased from ₹3.7 lakh crore in FY 2020 to ₹13.5 lakh 
crore in FY 2025, and further to ₹16.94 lakh crore in FY 
2026, reflecting a CAGR of approximately 29%. More 
than 61% of AIFs have been registered in the last four-
and-a-half years, highlighting the rapid expansion of the 
ecosystem.
Several structural trends are supporting growth in private 
markets:
•	
Increasing participation from domestic investors, 
family offices and institutional capital pools
•	
Growing demand for private credit as companies 
seek flexible financing solutions
•	
Rising allocations to commercial real estate through 
yield-oriented and income-generating strategies
•	
Expansion of venture debt as startups seek non-
dilutive capital alongside equity funding
•	
Stronger interest in private equity opportunities driven 
by India's favourable economic and entrepreneurial 
landscape
With AIF commitments projected to reach ₹53–65 
lakh crore by FY 2030, private markets are expected to 
remain one of the fastest-growing segments within India's 
managed investments industry, supported by growing 
domestic capital, increasing investor awareness and 
expanding access to alternative asset classes.

growth in alternative assets, increasing trading activity, technological advancement and an evolving regulatory framework.

remains significant scope for broader participation from 
investors across Europe, the Middle East and Asia-Pacific.

entrepreneurship, corporate growth, infrastructure development and wealth creation. Supported by deepening

significant capital formation markets across equity, debt and alternative financing channels.

in capital formation, reinforcing its position as one of 
the world’s most active fundraising platforms. FY 2026

a growth of 9.5% over the previous year. Activity was led 
by the mainboard segment, where 109 IPOs raised nearly 
₹1.7 Tn, accounting for the majority of funds mobilised 
during the year.

3. Asset Managers Outsourcing Non-Core 
Functions to Focus on Growth
Institutional investors, asset managers, AIFs, PMS platforms 
and global investors are increasingly seeking to focus on 
their core investment and distribution activities rather 
than managing operational and regulatory processes 
in-house. As a result, there is growing demand for 
outsourced solutions spanning custody, settlements, 
fund administration, reporting, compliance support and 
investor servicing.
This trend is driving greater adoption of specialised 
asset servicing platforms that offer scale, operational 
expertise, technology infrastructure and risk management 
capabilities, enabling clients to improve efficiency while 
reducing operational complexity.
4. Product Innovation Expanding the Asset 
Services Opportunity
The rapid growth of new investment structures such as 
AIFs, PMS, ETFs, REITs, InvITs, SIFs, structured products 
and debt-market instruments is expanding the scope 
of asset servicing. Each product category brings unique 
operational, reporting and regulatory requirements, 
increasing demand for integrated and technology-enabled 
custody and administration solutions.
As investment products become more sophisticated, 
asset servicing providers are increasingly required to 
support complex workflows across multiple asset classes 
and fund structures.
5. Maturing Capital Market – Increasing 
Volumes, Liquidity and Complexity
India’s capital markets are becoming increasingly 
transaction-intensive, supported by deeper participation 
in equities, derivatives and algorithmic trading strategies. 
While regulatory measures have sought to strengthen 
investor protection and curb excessive speculation, 
derivatives continue to play an important role in market 
liquidity, price discovery and risk management.
The increasing scale of market activity is driving demand 
for robust clearing, collateral management, margin 
monitoring, settlement and reconciliation infrastructure, 
making operational efficiency and risk control critical 
differentiators for asset servicing providers.
6. Regulatory Evolution - Asset Services 
Becoming a Strategic Enabler of Capital 
Markets
As India’s financial markets deepen, regulatory frameworks 
are evolving across investor protection, risk management, 
reporting standards, settlement processes and operational 
resilience.
Increasing oversight across market participants, 
investment vehicles and intermediaries is driving greater 
focus on compliance, governance and transparency.
In this environment, Asset Services is moving beyond 
traditional safekeeping and settlement execution to 
play a more strategic role in enabling market access, 
supporting complex fund structures, managing regulatory 
requirements and facilitating faster settlement cycles.
Technology-led platforms with strong compliance, 
reporting and data capabilities are becoming critical 
partners for institutions navigating regulatory complexity 
and scaling participation in India’s capital markets.

2. Private Deals Outlook Remains Constructive 
(M&A, PE)
India’s private equity and venture capital ecosystem 
demonstrated resilience and continued momentum 
in 2025 despite a challenging global macroeconomic 
environment. As per Private Equity and Venture Capital 
Trendbook 2026, total investments reached USD 60.7 
billion across 1,475 deals, marking an 8% increase in value 
and 9% growth in deal volume, making it the second-
highest year on record. Growth and start-up investments 
led the recovery, with deal volumes rising 56% and 19%, 
respectively, while sectoral concentration remained stable 
with the top five sectors – financial services, infrastructure, 
real estate, technology and e-commerce – accounting 
for ~72% of total investments. Real assets (infrastructure 
and real estate) continued to play a significant role, 
contributing over one-third of overall capital deployment.
Exit activity remained robust, with total exits reaching 
USD 32.9 billion across 257 deals, up 17% YoY, driven 
primarily by a sharp rebound in strategic exits, which grew 
211% to account for nearly half of total exit value. Fundraising 
activity also strengthened significantly, with funds raised 
reaching an all-time high of USD 23.2 billion across 123 
fundraises, reflecting strong investor confidence in India’s 
long-term growth story. While near-term deployment 
may remain measured amid global uncertainties and 
valuation gaps, the industry outlook remains constructive, 
supported by strong economic fundamentals, a robust IPO 
pipeline and increasing investor participation.
3. Growing Domestic Capital Fuelling Capital 
Market Participation
India’s capital markets have witnessed a structural shift 
in the composition of investment flows, with domestic 
capital emerging as an increasingly important source of 
market liquidity and stability. Historically, market direction 
was heavily influenced by foreign institutional investor 
(FII/FPI) flows. However, the rapid growth of mutual funds, 
insurance companies, pension funds, family offices, and 
retail investors has created a much larger and more 
resilient domestic investor base.

Company Performance and Strategic

Positioned at the intersection of trust, expertise and scale, 
we have emerged as one of India’s leading integrated 
wealth management firms, managing over ₹4.5 lakh crore 
of client assets. Serving a diverse clientele that includes 
individuals, institutions, CXOs and family offices, we offer 
a comprehensive suite of solutions across investment 
advisory, portfolio management, estate planning, lending 
and broking.
Beyond wealth management, our integrated platform 
encompasses 
an 
alternatives-focussed 
asset

services and capital markets franchises. This diversified 
yet synergistic ecosystem enables us to address the 
evolving financial needs of clients.
Nuvama’s Core Competencies
1. Marquee Promoter Support and Experienced 
Leadership
Backed by PAG, a leading global investment firm with over 
USD 57 billion in AUM and deep institutional expertise, 
we benefit from strategic support that strengthens 
our platform. This is complemented by an experienced 
leadership team with a proven track record across market 
cycles, enabling disciplined execution and long-term 
value creation. Together, global expertise and seasoned 
leadership provide Nuvama with a strong foundation for 
sustainable growth.
2. Integrated Ecosystem with Proven Scale and 
Early-Mover Advantage
Over the past two decades, we have built a comprehensive 
and scalable financial services ecosystem spanning 
Wealth Management, Asset Management, Asset Services 
and Capital Markets. This integrated platform enables 
us to address a wide spectrum of client needs through 
a single relationship, creating meaningful cross-segment 
synergies and a differentiated value proposition. Our 
hybrid model combines deep relationship-led advisory 
with advanced digital capabilities, enhancing client 
experience while supporting scalable growth across 
segments. As an early entrant in several of our businesses, 
we have benefited from over 15 years of investment in 
people, capabilities and infrastructure, allowing us to 
establish leadership positions, achieve scale and create 
sustainable competitive advantages across our operating 
segments.
3. Diversified Clientele with Pan-India Presence
We serve a diversified client base spanning Affluent & 
HNI, UHNI, Corporate, and Institutional segments across 
our businesses. As of March 31, 2026, we serve over 
1.3 million Affluent and HNI clients, along with 4,750+ UHNI 
clients and family offices, reflecting the depth and scale 
of our franchise. We have established a strong presence 
across 500+ locations, supported by a network of over 
75 branches, ~1,250 RMs and ~8,000 active External 
Wealth Managers, enabling broad market coverage and 
client access.
Our asset management business segment served more 
than 4,900 investors, while the capital markets business 
segment catered to over 1,000+ institutional and corporate 
clients as of March 31, 2026. Our total client assets stood at 
₹ 4.5+ lakh crore as of March 31, 2026, registering a CAGR 
of 23% over the past five years, underscoring sustained 
growth and client trust.
4. Diversified Revenue Streams and Strong 
Capital Position
We have delivered consistent growth in revenues and 
profitability over the past five years, reflecting the strength 
of our diversified business model. Our multi-stream 
revenue base provides stability and resilience, supporting 
secular growth while mitigating the impact of market 
volatility. Supported by a strong capital position, we 
remain well-capitalised to pursue growth opportunities, 
invest in capabilities and deliver resilient performance 
across market cycles.
5. Robust Technology Platform
We leverage technology to deliver a seamless and 
differentiated client experience. Our full-stack digital 
platform provides end-to-end capabilities across 
the value chain, including digital onboarding, straight-
through processing, client servicing, engagement and 
portfolio reporting. This technology backbone also 
enhances operational efficiency and scalability, while 
equipping relationship managers and external partners 
with advanced tools to deliver personalised, insight-led 
advisory.
5. Debt Markets Emerging as an Important 
Financing Channel
India’s fixed income market has undergone significant 
structural expansion over the past few years, creating 
a larger opportunity set for issuers, investors, and 
intermediaries. Outstanding government securities have 
nearly doubled from ₹61 lakh crore in FY 2019 to ₹125 
lakh crore in FY 2026, while the corporate bond market 
has expanded from ₹31 lakh crore to ₹57 lakh crore over 
the same period. Secondary market liquidity has also 
improved materially, with average daily trading volumes 
in G-Secs rising from approximately ₹300 billion to ₹600 
billion and corporate bond volumes increasing from ₹57 
billion to ₹88 billion.
Regulatory initiatives aimed at attracting foreign 
capital – including greater market access for FPIs, tax and 
operational reforms, FCNR(B) incentives, and concessional 
ECB funding facilities – are expected to further deepen 
debt markets, broaden the investor base, and drive higher 
issuance activity.

B)	 Internal Control Systems and 
Adequacy
	
We maintain a robust internal control framework, 
including comprehensive internal financial controls, 
aligned with the scale, nature and complexity of our 
business. Our internal financial controls system is 
designed to ensure operational efficiency, reliability 
of financial and operational information, safeguarding 
of assets, prevention and detection of fraud, and 
compliance with applicable laws and regulations.
	
The internal control system operates on the principle 
of three lines of defence. The first line comprises 
business, operations and technology functions, 
responsible for implementing controls and managing 
risks. The second line includes risk management and 
compliance functions, providing policy oversight 
and ensuring control effectiveness. The third line, 
internal audit, operates independently to evaluate 
the adequacy and effectiveness of these controls.
	
We undertake periodic internal audits, supported by 
an independent external firm, with comprehensive 
coverage across key functions including operations, 
risk, compliance, technology and finance. Audit 
findings and corrective actions, including those 
relating to subsidiaries, are reviewed by the Audit 
Committee on a quarterly basis.
	
This framework provides reasonable assurance on the 
effectiveness of our internal controls and governance 
processes.
C)	 Governance & Compliance
	
During the year, we continued to strengthen our 
enterprise-wide compliance, governance, and risk 
management framework through technology-driven 
initiatives, enhanced supervisory mechanisms, and 
robust internal controls. A structured programme was 
initiated for implementation of the Digital Personal 
Data Protection Act (DPDPA), and formation of a cross-
functional team to drive regulatory preparedness. We 
implemented multiple automation initiatives across 
critical processes to enhance operational efficiency, 
accuracy, and resilience, while also undertaking a 
comprehensive review of its risk framework and 
policies to align with evolving regulatory requirements 
and market conditions.
	
The surveillance framework was further enhanced 
through technology-enabled improvements in 
regulatory alert management and inter-segment 
surveillance capabilities to facilitate proactive 
identification of potential market abuse. We continued 
to evaluate the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) to 
strengthen risk management and surveillance through 
advanced analytics and monitoring capabilities.

RISK MANAGEMENT
Risk is an inherent and inseparable part of any business 
environment. The Company recognises that, while risks 
cannot be entirely eliminated, they can be effectively 
identified, assessed, monitored and mitigated through 
a structured and proactive approach. Accordingly, risk 
management forms an integral part of the Company’s 
corporate governance and decision-making framework 
and is aimed at safeguarding long-term value creation, 
financial resilience and operational continuity.
The Company has in place a Board-approved Risk 
Management Policy, which provides the overarching 
framework for identification, assessment, monitoring and 
mitigation of internal and external risks. These include, inter 
alia, financial, operational, sectoral, technological, cyber 
security, regulatory, reputational, environmental and other 
emerging risks. The Policy also ensures that appropriate 
systems, controls, escalation mechanisms and reporting 
structures are established and maintained across the 
organisation. Further, business continuity planning and risk 
response strategies are embedded into both day-to-day 
operations and strategic business planning.
To strengthen risk governance, the Company has 
adopted a “Four Lines of Defence” model. The first line 
of defence comprises of the business and operational 
teams, supported by technology and process controls, 
who are responsible for managing and owning risks within 
their respective functions. The second line of defence 
consists of the risk management and compliance 
functions, which independently oversee risk exposures, 
monitor adherence to established frameworks and 
support effective implementation of controls. The third 
line of defence includes the internal audit, external audit 
and surveillance functions which periodically assess the 
adequacy and effectiveness of internal controls and 
identify areas requiring improvement. The fourth line of 
defence rests with the Risk Management Committee and 
Board of Directors, which provide strategic oversight and 
periodically review the adequacy and effectiveness of the 
Company’s risk management framework.
The Company follows an Enterprise Risk Management 
(“ERM”) approach to ensure continuous identification, 
categorisation, assessment and prioritisation of risks. This 
framework is supported by the use of Key Risk Indicators 
(“KRIs”) for ongoing monitoring and timely escalation of 
material risk exposures. Risk ownership is clearly defined 
and mitigation plans are periodically reviewed to assess 
their effectiveness and residual risk impact. In addition, 
all new products, processes and business initiatives are 
evaluated from a risk perspective and are subject to 
approvals from relevant internal committees, including 
those relating to Risk, Compliance, Operations and Product 
Governance, as applicable.
The Company also undertakes periodic internal audits 
and control reviews to ensure that its control environment 
remains robust, effective and responsive to the evolving 
risk landscape. The internal financial and operational 
control systems commensurate with the nature, scale and 
complexity of the Company’s business and are designed 
to support regulatory compliance, financial discipline, 
operational efficiency and sound governance practices.
During the year under review, the Risk Management 
Committee did not identify any risk which, in its opinion, 
may threaten the existence or going concern status of 
the Company.
The Company remains committed to continuously 
strengthening its risk management capabilities and 
fostering a culture of accountability, transparency, 
resilience and continuous vigilance across the organisation.

This Nomination and Remuneration Policy (‘Policy’) of 
Nuvama Wealth Management Limited (‘the Company’) 
is formulated as per the Companies Act, 2013 and 
the rules made thereunder (‘the Act’) and the SEBI 
(Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) 
Regulations, 2015, as amended from time to time 
(‘Listing Regulations’) and other applicable laws.
2.	 Objective and Purpose:
The objective and purpose of this Policy are:
i.	
To formulate the criteria for determining 
qualifications, competencies, positive attributes 
and independence for appointment/re-
appointment of a Director of the Company and 
guiding the Board of Directors (‘the Board’) and 
the Nomination and Remuneration Committee 
(‘the Committee’) in this regard;
ii.	
To recommend candidates for appointment as 
Directors and Senior Management Personnel 
(’SMP’);
iii.	
To establish and review succession plans of the 
Board and SMP;
iv.	
Formulation of criteria for evaluation of 
Independent Directors and the Board as a whole;
v.	
To recommend policy relating to appointment/
re-appointment and removal of Directors and 
SMP;
vi.	
To recommend policy relating to the 
remuneration of the Directors and SMP / other 
employees to the Board;
vii.	 To review, determine and approve corporate 
goals, compensation and objectives relevant to 
the compensation of the Whole-time Directors 
and SMPs evaluating their performance in light 
of those goals and objectives.

4. 	 General:
	
PART A: Appointment and removal of 
Directors, Key Managerial Personnel and 
Senior Management Personnel:
	
I.	
Appointment criteria and qualifications
	
a.	
The Committee shall ascertain the integrity, 
qualification, expertise and experience of 
the person identified for appointment as 
Director, Senior Management Personnel 
and recommend to the Board his/her 
appointment. In this regard, the Committee 
has discretion to decide whether 
qualification, expertise and experience 
possessed by a person is sufficient / 
satisfactory for the position.
	
b.	
A person to be appointed as Director, 
Senior Management Personnel should 
possess adequate qualification, expertise 
and experience for the position he/she is 
considered for.
	
c.	
A person to be appointed as Director, 
should possess impeccable reputation 
for integrity, deep expertise and insights 
in sectors/areas relevant to the Company, 
ability to contribute to the Company’s 
growth and complementary skills in relation 
to the other Board members.
	
d.	
For every appointment of an independent 
director, the Committee shall evaluate the 
balance of skills, knowledge and experience 
on the Board and on the basis of such 
evaluation, prepare a description of the role 
and capabilities required of an independent 
director. The person recommended for such 
role shall meet the criteria laid down and 
should possess skills and other disciplines 
related to Company’s business.
	
e.	
The Company shall appoint or continue 
the employment of a person as managing 
director /whole-time director and non-
executive Director who has not attained the 
maximum age of retirement as prescribed 
under Applicable Laws.
	
f.	
A whole-time KMP of the Company shall 
not hold office in more than one company 
except in its subsidiary company at the 
same time. However, a whole-time KMP can 
be appointed as a Director in any company, 
with the permission of the Board.
	
g.	
The Company shall not appoint any 
resigning Independent Director, as whole-
time director, unless a period of one year 
has elapsed from the date of resignation as 
an Independent Director.
	
h.	
The term/tenure of the Directors and Senior 
Management Personnel/ other employees 
shall be in accordance with the applicable 
Laws and their respective contracts/ 
terms of appointment (and shareholders 
and/or government approvals, wherever 
applicable).
	
II.	
Removal:
	
Due to reasons for any disqualification 
mentioned in the Act or Listing Regulations 
or any other applicable law, the Committee 
may recommend to the Board with reasons 
recorded in writing, removal of a Director and 
Senior Management Personnel subject to the 
provisions and compliance of the Act, Listing 
Regulations or any other applicable laws.
	
III.	 Retirement:
	
The Directors and Senior Management Personnel 
shall retire as per the applicable provisions of 
the Act, any other applicable law and relevant 
policies of the Company. The Board will have 
the discretion to retain the Directors and Senior 
Management Personnel in the same position / 
remuneration or otherwise, even after attaining 
the retirement age, for the benefit of the 
Company, subject to approvals as required under 
the Act, Regulations or any other applicable laws.

Key Managerial Personnel and Senior 
Management Personnel:

Remuneration of the Independent 
Directors & Non- executive Directors
	
•	
The Independent Directors & Non-
Executive Directors are eligible for sitting 
fees for attending the meetings of the 
Board and the various Committees thereof.
	
•	
The Independent Directors & Non-Executive 
Directors are also eligible for commission, 
subject to limits prescribed under the Act 
and the Rules framed there under.
	
•	
The Independent Directors are not eligible 
for stock options.

Conservation of Energy
The Company’s operations are not energy intensive, being 
a financial services organisation. Nevertheless, adequate 
measures have been initiated across all branches of 
the Company to reduce energy consumption, as the 
Company is committed to sustainable business practices 
by contributing to environment protection and considers 
energy conservation as one of the strong pillars of 
preserving natural resources.

energy:
	
The operations of the Company are not energy 
intensive; however, adequate measures have been 
undertaken to conserve energy wherever possible, 
resulting in a year-on-year reduction in total energy 
consumption and energy intensity.

alternate sources of energy:

services and, as such, its operations do not account

branches

56% of the Company’s total energy consumption 
being sourced from renewable energy

of electronic and electrical equipment, including 
laptops, computers, lighting systems and air-

transparency, integrity, accountability and equity.

corporate governance is not merely compliance, but 
a strategic enabler of transparency, accountability 
and long term value creation.

framework by aligning its business environment 
with the relevant laws and regulations applicable 
to the Company. The Company’s strong internal 
control framework ensures adherence to ethical and 
sustainable business practices, achieving desired 
outcomes consistent with the Company’s governance 
framework, which has been approved by the Board of 
Directors.
	
The Company recognises that Corporate 
Governance is an evolving journey. Accordingly, 
the Company remains committed to continuous 
improvement through effective oversight, proactive 
risk management and alignment with our long-term 
strategic objectives. Our governance framework is 
designed to meet the expectations of our investors, 
regulators and other stakeholders, while ensuring that 
our business conduct consistently reflects our core 
values.
	
Building on the foundation laid last year, the Company 
continues to embed the EFG values—Excellence in 
Execution, Fairness and Growth into its organizational 
culture. These values, which emphasize ownership, 
agility, respect, integrity and entrepreneurial 
innovation, have become integral to the way we 
operate and make decisions.
	
The Company continuously reviews and strengthens 
the governance practices, benchmarking itself 
against the leading standards and best-governed 
companies. Through these combined efforts, we 
ensure our values are not only understood but 
actively practiced every day, creating a people-first 
and future-oriented culture.
2.	 BOARD OF DIRECTORS
	
The Board of Directors (‘Board’) comprises of 
experienced professionals from diverse backgrounds, 
bringing together a broad spectrum of expertise, 
knowledge and industry experience. This diversity 
of skills, perspectives and competencies enables 
the Board to make informed, balanced and strategic 
decisions while effectively discharging its governance 
responsibilities
	
The Board provides strategic leadership and 
oversight to the Company, with focus on driving 
sustainable long-term value creation for Members 
while balancing the interests of other stakeholders. 
In discharging its fiduciary duties, the Board ensures 
that the affairs of the Company are conducted in a 
prudent, ethical and transparent manner, consistent 
with the highest standards of Corporate Governance.
	
The Corporate Governance framework of the 
Company is based on an effective and Independent 
Board, Board Composition, separation of the Board’s 
supervisory role from the Senior Management team 
and Board Committees and its charter, as required 
under applicable Laws/Regulations.
(a)	 Composition of the Board
	
The Board comprises of highly experienced persons 
of repute, eminence and has a good and diverse 
mix of Executive and Non-Executive Directors with 
50% being Independent Directors including an

(‘the Act’) and Listing Regulations. Profile of our

Corporate Governance Report
	
The Board is the highest authority and custodian 
for the governance and drives Company’s business 
in the right direction. The Board is responsible 
for setting the Company’s strategic direction and 
overseeing the execution of its business objectives. 
Its responsibilities include reviewing and approving 
the Company’s strategy, annual operating plans, 
business plans and budgets; monitoring operational 
and financial performance; and overseeing significant 
investments, acquisitions, divestments, capital 
allocation decisions and other strategic initiatives. 
The Board also plays a key role in strengthening the 
Company’s governance framework and ensuring 
continued alignment with applicable regulatory 
requirements and evolving best governance 
practices.
	
The Board oversees the effectiveness of the 
Company’s risk management framework and 
internal control environment, including internal 
financial controls, operational controls and 
compliance systems to ensure that material risks 
are appropriately identified, assessed, managed and 
mitigated. It is also responsible for the appointment, 
evaluation, remuneration and succession planning 
of the Managing Director, Key Managerial Personnel 
and Senior Management, while ensuring that 
compensation structures support the Company’s 
long-term objectives and Members interests.
	
The Board further safeguards the integrity of the 
Company’s financial reporting and disclosure 
processes and oversees the effectiveness of the 
independent audit function and compliance with 
applicable laws, regulations and standards.
	
The Board also provides oversight on the Company’s 
Environmental, Social and Governance (‘ESG’) 
framework and Corporate Social Responsibility (‘CSR’) 
initiatives, ensuring that sustainability considerations 
are integrated into the Company’s strategy, risk 
management processes and business operations. It 
periodically reviews the Company’s ESG priorities, 
sustainability goals, performance and oversees 
initiatives relating to environmental stewardship, 
responsible business conduct, employee well-being, 
diversity and inclusion, community development and 
stakeholder engagement. The Board further ensures 
compliance with applicable ESG-related disclosure 
requirements and monitors the effectiveness and 
impact of CSR programmes undertaken by the 
Company in alignment with its commitment to 
sustainable and inclusive growth.
	
In addition, the Board periodically evaluates its own 
effectiveness, as well as that of its Committees and 
individual Directors, to strengthen governance and 
enhance Board performance. The Board fosters 
constructive engagement with Members and other 
stakeholders, promotes responsible and sustainable 
business practices and ensures that adequate 
Directors’ and Officers’ Liability Insurance coverage 
is maintained. It also ensures that Directors discharge 
their duties independently and objectively, free from 
any conflicts that may impair their judgment or 
compromise the interests of the Company.

Corporate Governance, the Company has maintained 
50% Independent Directors on its Board, exceeding 
the minimum requirement of one-third prescribed

are related to each other.

were held as against the statutory requirement of four

(c)	 Board Procedures
	
To facilitate effective planning and ensuring the 
availability of all Directors, the dates for Board 
Meetings for the ensuing financial year are scheduled 
well in advance. The proposed dates for the Meetings 
are then formally communicated to all Directors, 
enabling them to align their commitments and 
support meaningful participation in the Meetings.
	
The Board meets at least once a quarter to review the 
quarterly financial results and other agenda items. 
Additional Meetings are called, when necessary, to 
consider urgent business matters. There are minimum 
four Meetings of the Board in a financial year with a 
maximum gap of 120 days between two consecutive 
Meetings. In case of business exigencies or matter 
of urgency, resolutions are passed by circulation, 
as permitted by law and the same are noted at the 
subsequent Board Meeting.
	
All Committee recommendations placed before the 
Board during the year under review were unanimously 
accepted by the Board.
	
The quorum for the meeting of the Board is one-
third of the Board or three Directors, whichever is 
higher, including at least one Independent Director. 
During the year under review, the requisite quorum 
was present for all Board Meetings. Attendance 
at Board Meetings remained consistently strong, 
with participation well above the minimum quorum 
requirements for all Board Meetings.
	
The Board devotes its significant time in evaluation 
of current and potential strategic issues and reviews 
Company’s business plans, corporate strategy and 
risk management issues based on the markets it 
operates in and in light of the global industry trends 
and developments to help achieve its strategic goals.
	
In special and exceptional circumstances, 
consideration of additional or supplementary items 
are taken up with the approval of the Chairperson 
and majority of the Directors present in the Meeting, 
including one Independent Director.
	
Senior Management Personnel are invited to the 
Board/ Committee Meetings to provide additional 
inputs on the items being discussed by the Board/ 
Committees as and when necessary. The Managing 
Director and CEO apprises the Board on the overall 
performance of the Company, followed by the 
detailed presentation by the Chief Financial Officer 
and other Senior Executives of the Company.
	
The Meetings of the Board are generally held at the 
Registered Office of the Company. The Company 
offers the facility of video conferencing as prescribed 
under Section 173(2) of the Act read with Rule 3 of 
the Companies (Meetings of Board and its Powers) 
Rules, 2014, thereby saving resources and cost to the 
Company as well as the valued time of the Directors. 
The Board Meetings are either attended by the 
Directors in person or through video conferencing.

The Board has access to all material information 
relating to the Company and its subsidiaries, including 
strategic priorities and business plans, the Annual 
Operating Plan, Financial Performance and Business 
Outlook, Budgets and Forecasts, Minutes of Meetings 
of the Board and its Committees, as well as those of 
the Boards of subsidiary companies. Board Meetings 
are governed by structured agenda.
	
The Board is furnished with timely, relevant and 
comprehensive information to facilitate informed 
decision-making and enable the effective discharge 
of its fiduciary, strategic and oversight responsibilities. 
The Board is also regularly apprised of material 
investments, acquisitions, strategic partnerships 
and other significant business initiatives; if any, in 
financial obligations by or to the Company; significant 
litigation, regulatory actions; developments in 
technology, cybersecurity, human resources and 
other key operational areas; and compliance 
with applicable statutory, regulatory and listing 
requirements. Further, the Board receives periodic 
updates on risk management, governance matters, 
investor relations and stakeholder service-related 
issues, ensuring that it remains adequately informed 
of all material developments that may impact the 
Company’s operations, performance, reputation or 
long-term sustainability. The Board is periodically 
updated on regulatory changes, amendments and 
compliance obligations.
	
The detailed Agenda together with the relevant 
notes are circulated to the Board and Committee 
members in advance. All Agenda items are backed

Board provides the overall framework for the 
functioning of the Internal Audit function and 
defines its roles, responsibilities, authority and 
operating methodology. The Policy also sets out 
the approach for preparation of the Risk-Based 
Internal Audit (‘RBIA’) Plan and the risk-based 
rating methodology for audit observations, 
thereby ensuring a structured and consistent 
assessment of risks and controls across the 
organisation.
	
	
The Audit Committee reviews and approves the 
RBIA Plan annually, which is developed in line 
with applicable regulatory requirements and 
leading governance practices. The plan is based 
on an independent and comprehensive risk 
assessment covering the Company’s businesses, 
functions, processes and locations. Through 
a systematic and risk-focused approach, the 
Internal Audit function provides independent 
assurance on the adequacy and effectiveness 
of the Company’s internal control environment, 
risk management framework and governance 
processes, while also identifying opportunities

The Company recognizes communication as a 
key element to the overall Corporate Governance 
framework and therefore emphasizes on prompt, 
continuous, efficient and relevant communication.
	
Financial Results:

Financial Results are filed with the Stock Exchanges as 
well as uploaded on the website of the Company. The 
same are also published in newspapers in Financial 
Express (English) and Navashakti (Marathi) and are 
also available on the website of the Company.

Post the quarterly results, earnings conference call is 
organized by the Company which provides a platform 
for the management to answer questions and provide 
clarifications to investors and analysts. Detailed 
presentations are made to investors and analysts. 
The audio recordings and transcript of these earning 
calls are submitted to the Stock Exchanges and 
uploaded on the website of the Company.
	
The Company hosts Investor/Analyst meets with 
institutional investors. Presentations made to 
institutional investors and financial analysts on the 
financial results are submitted to the stock exchanges 
and also uploaded on the Company’s website. No 
unpublished price sensitive information is discussed 
in meetings with institutional investors and analysts.
	
The Company continues to interact with all types 
of funds and investors in order to have a diversified 
Board of Members both in terms of geographical 
location and investment horizon. Official news 
releases/ media releases are generally submitted 
to the stock exchanges and also uploaded on the 
Company’s website.
	
Website:

dedicated section for Investors, which is available on 
the website of the Company i.e. https://www.nuvama.

terms of reference of the Committee, Policies, 
financial information, statutory filings, shareholding 
information. In addition, various downloadable forms 
required to be executed by the Members have also 
been provided on the website of the Company in a 
user friendly form.
