Economy Overview
Global Economy: A Year of Tariffs, Technology 
and Tensions
FY 2026 was a defining year from a global economic 
perspective, shaped by significant developments across 
three critical fronts - trade, technology and geopolitics. 
The year began with a sharp escalation in trade policy, 
following the US announcement of ‘Liberation Day’ 
tariffs on April 2, 2025. This was followed by a period of 
heightened uncertainty, with tariff rates for some trading 
partners rising as high as 50%. Although the US Supreme 
Court struck down select tariffs, offering partial relief, 
the overall effective US tariff rate remained elevated at 
around 10%, levels not seen since the post-World War II

era, signalling the end of the prolonged phase of low global 
tariffs.
Alongside this, FY 2026 witnessed a step-change in 
technological disruption, led by rapid advancements in 
AI. Major AI firms such as Anthropic, Google, Meta and 
others accelerated the development of enterprise-
grade AI models, infrastructure and applications, pushing 
adoption into more critical use cases. This supported a 
sharp rise in AI-linked investment and created second-
order effects across global supply chains, driving demand 
for semiconductors, data centres and power capacity, 
while also raising concerns around labour displacement, 
particularly in services.
Geopolitical tensions further intensified during the year, 
culminating in a direct confrontation involving the US, 
Iran and Israel. The conflict led to the closure of the Strait 
of Hormuz, disrupting global supply chains and driving 
a sharp increase in crude oil prices and shipping costs, 
which heightened global volatility and further complicated 
the inflation outlook.
Despite overlapping shocks, the global economy remained 
relatively resilient in CY 2026, with world GDP growth 
projected at 3.1%, moderating from around 3.4% in CY 
2025, according to the International Monetary Fund’s 
World Economic Outlook, April 2026. However, growth 
trends remained uneven across regions. The US economy 
improved modestly to 2.3% in CY 2026 from 2.1% in CY 
2025, while China’s growth moderated to 4.4% from 5.0% 
and the Euro Area slowed to 1.1% from 1.4%.
Looking ahead, renewed tensions and intermittent 
escalations continue to create uncertainty around trade 
flows, energy markets and supply chains, with limited 
visibility on when conditions may fully normalise. While 
supply-side constraints could gradually unwind over 
time and the benefits of AI adoption are expected to 
increasingly translate into productivity gains, supporting 
medium-term growth, risks remain elevated. Any 
prolonged geopolitical disruptions or supply shock

s could 
spill over into broader demand weakness globally. In this 
environment, policy responses, structural reforms and 
balance sheet resilience will play a critical role in shaping 
the trajectory of global growth.
India: Anchoring Growth through Policy Support
In a year marked by global uncertainty, India stood out as 
a policy oasis, supported by coordinated monetary, fiscal 
and regulatory measures aimed at sustaining growth. 
Under the new RBI governor, monetary policy turned 
decisively accommodative, with cumulative repo rate 
cuts of 125 bps bringing the policy rate down to 5.25%, 
alongside liquidity support and regulatory easing. This 
was complemented by fiscal and tax measures focussed 
on consumption and ease of living, including relief in 
individual income-tax rates, GST rate rationalisation 
through simplified slabs and lower rates on several goods 
and services, as well as the removal of GST on individual 
life and health insurance premiums.
These measures gradually translated into improved 
domestic activity, with bank credit growth strengthening 
during the year and reaching 14.1% YoY by end-March 
2026, compared with 11.1% a year earlier, according to RBI 
data. High-frequency indicators, including automobile 
sales and other consumption-linked activity, also pointed 
to a gradual revival in underlying momentum. However, 
the recovery remained uneven, with corporate earnings 
staying under pressure across several sectors amid 
subdued demand conditions and global uncertainty.
Given the challenging external environment, geopolitical 
tensions and elevated tariffs weighed on India’s goods 
exports, which grew modestly by around 1% in FY 2026. 
Services exports remained resilient, rising by nearly 9% 
in USD terms, helping cushion the impact of subdued 
merchandise trade. However, global risk aversion, volatile 
capital markets and relatively attractive opportunities 
across other emerging markets contributed to foreign 
portfolio investor outflo

ws and weaker capital inflows 
into India. Despite these headwinds, India remained 
among the fastest-growing major economies, with real 
GDP growth rising to 7.7% in FY 2026 from 7.1% in FY 2025, 
according to MoSPI’s Provisional Estimates released on 
June 5, 2026. Inflation dynamics were also favourable, 
with headline CPI easing from 4.6% in FY 2025 to around 
4.0% in FY 2026, supported by softer food inflation. On 
the external policy front, India continued to strengthen 
trade linkages, including the India–UK trade agreement 
and ongoing engagement with the US and other key 
partners, supporting export competitiveness and supply 
chain diversification.
Looking ahead, while INR depreciation could enhance 
India’s export competitiveness, it may also raise import 
costs, particularly for crude oil and other key inputs, 
thereby adding to inflationary pressures and weighing on 
the broader macroeconomic outlook. Domestic liquidity 
conditions are also expected to remain comfortable, 
supported by the RBI’s continued liquidity measures, 
which is also reflected from the fact that liquidity has 
remained in surplus despite pressure on India’s BoP, which 
is a historic anomaly.
Overall, India’s macroeconomic resilience remains 
underpinned by a strong corporate balance sheet, a 
credible policy framework, ongoing structural reforms, 
rising formalisation, rapid digitalisation, and sustained 
investments in infrastructure and manufacturing are likely 
to anchor long-term growth. In an increasingly fragmented 
global economy, India continues to strengthen its position 
as a key driver of global growth.
Industry Overview and Outlook
India’s long-term growth story is being shaped by a 
powerful convergence of structural forces that extend 
well beyond cyclical economic trends. Strong economic 
growth, rising disposable incomes, increasing formalisation, 
digital adoption and progressive regulatory advancements 
are reshaping how capital is created, allocated and 
compoun

ded across the economy. At the same time, a 
high domestic savings base, accelerating financialisation 
of household wealth and growing participation of 
domestic investors in capital markets are strengthening 
the foundations of sustainable growth.
These structural tailwinds are expected to drive a 
significant expansion in wealth creation over the coming 
decade. As per BCG’s Global Wealth Report 2026, India 
is expected to add over USD 2 Tn in financial wealth by 
2030, growing at a 12% CAGR (Affluent and emerging HNW 
segment with investable assets above USD 250,000). This 
growth is supported by deeper financial inclusion, rising 
investor participation and an increasingly mature financial 
ecosystem, keeping India among the most compelling 
long-term wealth opportunities globally.

2. High Domestic Savings Supporting Long-
Term Capital Formation
India’s consistently high savings rate reflects one of the 
country’s most important structural strengths – a large 
and growing pool of domestic capital. As per World Bank, 
Gross domestic savings increased from 13% of GDP in 1975 
to a peak of 37% in 2007 and currently stand at around 
30%, comfortably above the global average of 26.2%. This 
strong savings culture provides a durable foundation for 
capital formation and long-term economic growth.

3. Financialisation of Household Savings
India’s household savings landscape is undergoing a 
gradual but meaningful transformation, with

savings 
increasingly moving beyond traditional physical assets 
such as real estate and gold towards financial assets. 
Rising incomes, greater financial awareness, wider product 
availability and improved digital access are encouraging 
greater participation in mutual funds, insurance, pension 
products and other market-linked investment avenues.
Despite this progress, India continues to have one of the 
lowest shares of financial assets in overall household 
wealth relative to many major economies, where financial 
assets account for 25.8% of the total gross savings. 
This gap highlights the substantial headroom for further 
financialisation as incomes rise, financial literacy improves 
and capital market participation deepens. At the same 
time, product innovation is broadening the investible 
universe by converting traditionally illiquid or physical 
assets into accessible, regulated and market-linked 
instruments. REITs and InvITs are enabling investors 
to participate in income-generating real estate and 
infrastructure assets, while ETFs are providing low-cost, 
transparent exposure to asset classes such as gold 
and equities. This evolution is helping deepen financial 
markets, improve diversification and create new avenues 
for household savings to participate in India’s long-term 
growth story.

and Efficiency
Over the past decade, India’s digital transformation has 
reshaped how citizens access services, transact, learn 
and participate in the economy. Supported by one of the 
world’s largest Digital Public Infrastructure ecosystems, 
initiatives such as Aadhaar, UPI, DigiLocker and the JAM 
trinity (Jan Dhan Accounts, Aadhaar and Mobile) have 
significantly enhanced financial

inclusion, reduced friction 
in service delivery, and improved transparency across 
the economy. As per The Digital India report by PIB, as of 
March 2026, over 109 crore people had internet access, 
broadband subscribers exceeded 106 crore, and UPI 
processed more than 24,000 crore transactions during 
FY 2026, underscoring the scale of digital adoption across 
both urban and rural India.
Beyond improving productivity and reducing transaction 
costs, Digital India is fostering financial inclusion, 
broadening access to investment and banking services, 
and creating a more connected and efficient economic 
ecosystem. As digital adoption continues to deepen, it 
is expected to remain a key enabler of economic growth, 
financialisation and wealth creation.
5. Robust Regulatory Oversight Strengthening 
Market Confidence
India’s financial services industry is entering a more 
mature phase, with rising participation across mutual 
funds, alternatives, capital markets, insurance, lending and 
wealth solutions.
As the ecosystem becomes larger, more digital and 
increasingly interconnected, regulatory oversight has 
also evolved, with institutions such as SEBI, RBI, IRDAI and 
AMFI playing an important role in strengthening market 
conduct, risk management, transparency and investor 
protection standards.
Recent regulatory actions have covered a broad set of 
areas, including tighter oversight of derivatives trading, 
enhanced margin and collateral frameworks, greater 
transparency in AIFs and PMS, sharper disclosure 
requirements for listed companies and intermediaries, 
and stronger governance expectations across market 
participants. SEBI’s continued focus on retail investor 
protection, particularly in the equity derivatives segment, 
reflects the need to balance rapid market deepening with 
orderly and sustainable participation.
Beyond securities markets, regulatory tightening has also 
been visible across banking and insurance. RBI’s evolving 
prudential framework fo

r project finance, liquidity and 
funding norms is aimed at strengthening balance-
sheet resilience and harmonising risk standards across 
regulated entities. Similarly, IRDAI’s consolidated insurance 
regulations, including sharper product governance, 
surrender-value disclosures and the development of 
digital market infrastructure such as Bima Sugam, are 
intended to improve customer outcomes and expand 
insurance penetration.
For the industry, this environment raises compliance 
expectations and near-term adaptation costs, but it 
also creates a stronger foundation for long-term growth. 
Well-governed and well-capitalised platforms are likely 
to benefit as regulatory intensity favours transparency, 
institutionalisation and scale. Over time, a robust 
regulatory architecture should deepen trust, improve

6. Demographic Dividend and Intergenerational 
Wealth Transfer
India’s wealth management opportunity is being 
structurally reshaped by two powerful long-term forces: 
a young, aspirational population entering its prime 
earning years and a large intergenerational transfer 
of wealth. Together, these trends are expected to 
expand household wealth creation, deepen demand for 
professional advice and create a broader opportunity 
set for integrated wealth management platforms. 
India’s demographic dividend represents a unique 
opportunity to support long-term economic growth and 
expan

d household wealth creation.
According to the United Nations World Population 
Prospects 2024, India is home to about 1.46 billion 
people in 2025, with nearly 68% of the population in the 
working-age group of 15–64 years and a median age of 
approximately 29 years, making it one of the youngest 
major economies globally. As this large working-age 
cohort enters higher income and savings phases, it is 
expected to create a sizeable opportunity for wealth 
managers by increasing the need for financial planning, 
investment advisory and long-term wealth solutions. 
  
At the same time, India is entering a phase of significant 
wealth succession and family wealth formalisation. Reports 
indicate that around USD 1.3-1.5 Tn of wealth may transfer 
to the next generation over the next decade, while the 
number of Indian family offices has expanded sharply from 
around 45 in 2018 to nearly 300 by 2024. This creates a 
strong demand for integrated platforms that can support 
succession planning, portfolio diversification, governance, 
estate planning, alternatives, philanthropy, and global 
allocation.

2. Accelerating Shift Towards Capital Market 
Led Investment Solutions
Investor preferences continue to evolve from traditional 
transaction-based investing towards professionally 
managed and advisory-led solutions. Sustained domestic 
capital market participation, increasing financial literacy, 
and the growing complexity of investment decisions have 
accelerated demand for managed products across wealth 
segments.
PMS, AIF, mutual funds, structured products, and 
discretionary portfolio solutions continue to gain 
market share as investors seek professional expertise, 
diversification, and risk-adjusted returns. This structural 
shift is also supporting the industry’s transition from 
distribution-led models towards recurring fee-based 
advisory relationships, resulting in stronger client 
engagement and more predictable revenue streams for 
wealth managers.
3. Offshore Investing Emerging as a Key Wealth 
Management Theme
Global diversification is increasingly becoming an 
important portfolio consideration for Indian HNIs and 
UHNIs, driven by the need to access a broader opportunity 
set, diversify geographic and currency exposure, and 
participate in global investment themes. As client wealth 
grows and investment sophistication increases, demand 
for offshore i

nvestment solutions continues to gain 
momentum.
This trend is enabled through established regulatory 
channels, such as the Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS) 
for individuals and the Overseas Direct Investment (ODI) 
framework for entities, which allow structured, compliant 
access to international markets and offshore investment 
structures. These routes are increasingly used by HNIs, 
UHNIs, and family offices for global portfolio allocation, 
alternative investments, and overseas structuring.
The development of GIFT City and the International 
Financial Services Centre (IFSC) ecosystem has further 
strengthened India’s offshore wealth management 
infrastructure by providing a regulated platform for 
accessing global investment opportunities. Wealth 
managers are increasingly leveraging strategic partnerships 
with External Asset Managers (EAMs), international 
product providers, and global investment platforms 
to offer clients access to international equities, global 
fixed income, alternative investments, and discretionary 
portfolio solutions.

6. Technology and AI Transforming Wealth 
Management Delivery
Technology continues to reshape the wealth management 
value chain, enhancing efficiency, scalability, and client 
engagement. Digital onboarding, portfolio analytics, client 
reporting, and integrated advisory platforms have become 
key differentiators across the industry.

accelerating this transformation through personalised

The competitive landscape continues to evolve with 
participation from private banks, standalone wealth 
managers, boutique advisory firms, asset managers,

the entry of several new wealth management platforms

prospects.

platform expansion, technology investments, acquisitions,

relationship depth, firms are increasingly focussed on 
strengthening talent retention, technology capabilities, 
and differentiated service models to sustain growth and 
market share.

Capital Markets
India’s capital markets continue to play a critical role in channeling savings into productive investments, supporting 
entrepreneurship, corporate growth, infrastructure development and wealth creation. Supported by deepening 
financialisation, rising domestic participation and a growing investor base, India has emerged as one of the world’s most 
significant capital formation markets across equity, debt and alternative financing channels.
1. Primary Markets Supporting Capital 
Formation
India’s primary market continued to play a pivotal role 
in capital formation, reinforcing its position as one of 
the world’s most active fundraising platforms. FY 2026 
witnessed a record 366 IPOs, raising approximately ₹1.9 Tn, 
a growth of 9.5% over the previous year. Activity was led 
by the mainboard segment, where 109 IPOs raised nearly 
₹1.7 Tn, accounting for the majority of funds mobilised 
during the year.
The strong fundraising

environment was supported by 
robust participation across both mainboard and SME 
segments, reflecting growing investor confidence and 
continued demand for growth capital. While recent

3. Asset Managers Outsourcing Non-Core 
Functions to Focus on Growth
Institutional investors, asset managers, AIFs, PMS platforms 
and global investors are increasingly seeking to focus on 
their core investment and distribution activities rather 
than managing operational and regulatory processes 
in-house. As a result, there is growing demand for 
outsourced solutions spanning custody, settlements, 
fund administration, reporting, compliance support and 
investor servicing.
This trend is driving greater adoption of specialised 
asset servicing platforms that offer scale, operational 
expertise, technology infrastructure and risk management 
capabilities, enabling clients to improve efficiency while 
reducing operational complexity.
4. Product Innovation Expanding the Asset 
Services Opportunity
The rapid growth of new investment structures such as 
AIFs, PMS, ETFs, REITs, InvITs, SIFs, structured products 
and debt-market instruments is expanding the scope 
of asset servicing. Each product category brings unique 
operational, reporting and regulatory requirements, 
increasing demand for integrated and technology-enabled 
custody and administration solutions.
As investment products become more sophisticated, 
asset servicing providers are increasingly required to 
support complex workflows across multiple asset classes 
and fund structures.
5. Maturing Capital Market – Increasing 
Volumes, Liquidity and Complexity
India’s capital markets are becoming increasingly 
transaction-intensive, supported by deeper participation 
in equities, derivatives and algorithmic trading strategies. 
While regulatory measures have sought to strengthen 
investor protection and curb excessive speculation, 
derivat

ives continue to play an important role in market 
liquidity, price discovery and risk management.
The increasing scale of market activity is driving demand 
for robust clearing, collateral management, margin 
monitoring, settlement and reconciliation infrastructure, 
making operational efficiency and risk control critical 
differentiators for asset servicing providers.
6. Regulatory Evolution - Asset Services 
Becoming a Strategic Enabler of Capital 
Markets
As India’s financial markets deepen, regulatory frameworks 
are evolving across investor protection, risk management, 
reporting standards, settlement processes and operational 
resilience.
Increasing oversight across market participants, 
investment vehicles and intermediaries is driving greater 
focus on compliance, governance and transparency.
In this environment, Asset Services is moving beyond 
traditional safekeeping and settlement execution to 
play a more strategic role in enabling market access, 
supporting complex fund structures, managing regulatory 
requirements and facilitating faster settlement cycles.
Technology-led platforms with strong compliance, 
reporting and data capabilities are becoming critical 
partners for institutions navigating regulatory complexity 
and scaling participation in India’s capital markets.

2. Private Deals Outlook Remains Constructive 
(M&A, PE)
India’s private equity and venture capital ecosystem 
demonstrated resilience and continued momentum 
in 2025 despite a challenging global macroeconomic 
environment. As per Private Equity and Venture Capital 
Trendbook 2026, total investments reached USD 60.7 
billion across 1,475 deals, marking an 8% increase in value 
and 9% growth in deal volume, making it the second-
highest year on record. G

rowth and start-up investments 
led the recovery, with deal volumes rising 56% and 19%, 
respectively, while sectoral concentration remained stable 
with the top five sectors – financial services, infrastructure, 
real estate, technology and e-commerce – accounting 
for ~72% of total investments. Real assets (infrastructure 
and real estate) continued to play a significant role, 
contributing over one-third of overall capital deployment.
Exit activity remained robust, with total exits reaching 
USD 32.9 billion across 257 deals, up 17% YoY, driven 
primarily by a sharp rebound in strategic exits, which grew 
211% to account for nearly half of total exit value. Fundraising 
activity also strengthened significantly, with funds raised 
reaching an all-time high of USD 23.2 billion across 123 
fundraises, reflecting strong investor confidence in India’s 
long-term growth story. While near-term deployment 
may remain measured amid global uncertainties and 
valuation gaps, the industry outlook remains constructive, 
supported by strong economic fundamentals, a robust IPO 
pipeline and increasing investor participation.
3. Growing Domestic Capital Fuelling Capital 
Market Participation
India’s capital markets have witnessed a structural shift 
in the composition of investment flows, with domestic 
capital emerging as an increasingly important source of 
market liquidity and stability. Historically, market direction 
was heavily influenced by foreign institutional investor 
(FII/FPI) flows. However, the rapid growth of mutual funds, 
insurance companies, pension funds, family offices, and 
retail investors has created a much larger and more 
resilient domestic investor base.

Positioned at the intersection of trust, expertise and scale, 
we have emerged as one of India’s leading integrated 
wealth management firms, managing over ₹4.5 lakh crore

Nuvama’s Core Competencies
1. Marquee Promoter Support and Experienced 
Leadership
Backed by PAG, a leading global investment firm with over 
USD 57 billion in AUM and deep institutional expertise, 
we benefit from strategic support that strengthens 
our platform. This is complemented by an experienced 
leadership team with a proven track record across market 
cycles, enabling disciplined execution and long-term 
value creation. Together, global expertise and seasoned 
leadership provide Nuvama with a strong foundation for 
sustainable growth.
2. Integrated Ecosystem with Proven Scale and 
Early-Mover Advantage
Over the past two decades, we have built a comprehensive 
and scalable financial services ecosystem spanning 
Wealth Management, Asset Management, Asset Services 
and Capital Markets. This integrated platform enables 
us to address a wide spectrum of client needs through 
a single relationship, creating meaningful cross-segment 
synergies and a differentiated value proposition. Our 
hybrid model combines deep relationship-led advisory 
with advanced digital capabilities, enhancing client 
experience while supporting sca

lable growth across 
segments. As an early entrant in several of our businesses, 
we have benefited from over 15 years of investment in 
people, capabilities and infrastructure, allowing us to 
establish leadership positions, achieve scale and create 
sustainable competitive advantages across our operating 
segments.
3. Diversified Clientele with Pan-India Presence
We serve a diversified client base spanning Affluent & 
HNI, UHNI, Corporate, and Institutional segments across 
our businesses. As of March 31, 2026, we serve over 
1.3 million Affluent and HNI clients, along with 4,750+ UHNI 
clients and family offices, reflecting the depth and scale 
of our franchise. We have established a strong presence 
across 500+ locations, supported by a network of over 
75 branches, ~1,250 RMs and ~8,000 active External 
Wealth Managers, enabling broad market coverage and 
client access.
Our asset management business segment served more 
than 4,900 investors, while the capital markets business 
segment catered to over 1,000+ institutional and corporate 
clients as of March 31, 2026. Our total client assets stood at 
₹ 4.5+ lakh crore as of March 31, 2026, registering a CAGR 
of 23% over the past five years, underscoring sustained 
growth and client trust.
4. Diversified Revenue Streams and Strong 
Capital Position
We have delivered consistent growth in revenues and 
profitability over the past five years, reflecting the strength 
of our diversified business model. Our multi-stream 
revenue base provides stability and resilience, supporting 
secular growth while mitigating the impact of market 
volatility. Supported by a strong capital position, we 
remain well-capitalised to pursue growth opportunities, 
invest in capabilities and deliver resilient performance 
across market cycles.
5. Robust Technology Platform
We leverage technology to deliver a seamless and 
differentiated client experience. Our full-stack digital 
platform provides end-to-end capabilities across 
the value c

hain, including digital onboarding, straight-
through processing, client servicing, engagement and 
portfolio reporting. This technology backbone also 
enhances operational efficiency and scalability, while 
equipping relationship managers and external partners 
with advanced tools to deliver personalised, insight-led 
advisory.
5. Debt Markets Emerging as an Important 
Financing Channel
India’s fixed income market has undergone significant 
structural expansion over the past few years, creating 
a larger opportunity set for issuers, investors, and 
intermediaries. Outstanding government securities have 
nearly doubled from ₹61 lakh crore in FY 2019 to ₹125 
lakh crore in FY 2026, while the corporate bond market 
has expanded from ₹31 lakh crore to ₹57 lakh crore over 
the same period. Secondary market liquidity has also 
improved materially, with average daily trading volumes 
in G-Secs rising from approximately ₹300 billion to ₹600 
billion and corporate bond volumes increasing from ₹57 
billion to ₹88 billion.
Regulatory initiatives aimed at attracting foreign 
capital – including greater market access for FPIs, tax and 
operational reforms, FCNR(B) incentives, and concessional 
ECB funding facilities – are expected to further deepen 
debt markets, broaden the investor base, and drive higher 
issuance activity.

B)	 Internal Control Systems and 
Adequacy
	
We maintain a robust internal control framework, 
including comprehensive internal financial controls, 
aligned with the scale, nature and complexity of our 
business. Our internal financial controls system is 
designed to ensure operational efficiency, reliability 
of financial and operational information, safeguarding 
of assets, prevention and detection of fraud, and 
compliance with applicable laws and regulations.
	
The internal control system operates on the principle 
of three lines of defence. The first line comprises 
business, operations and technology functions, 
responsible for implementing controls and managing 
risks. The second line includes risk management and 
compliance functions, providing policy oversight 
and ensuring control effectiveness. The third line, 
internal audit, operates independently to evaluate 
the adequacy and effectiveness of these controls.
	
We undertake periodic internal audits, supported by 
an independent external firm, with comprehensive 
coverage across key functions including operations, 
risk, compliance, technology and finance. Audit 
findings and corrective actions, including those 
relating to subsidiaries, are revie

wed by the Audit 
Committee on a quarterly basis.
	
This framework provides reasonable assurance on the 
effectiveness of our internal controls and governance 
processes.
C)	 Governance & Compliance
	
During the year, we continued to strengthen our 
enterprise-wide compliance, governance, and risk 
management framework through technology-driven 
initiatives, enhanced supervisory mechanisms, and 
robust internal controls. A structured programme was 
initiated for implementation of the Digital Personal 
Data Protection Act (DPDPA), and formation of a cross-
functional team to drive regulatory preparedness. We 
implemented multiple automation initiatives across 
critical processes to enhance operational efficiency, 
accuracy, and resilience, while also undertaking a 
comprehensive review of its risk framework and 
policies to align with evolving regulatory requirements 
and market conditions.
	
The surveillance framework was further enhanced 
through technology-enabled improvements in 
regulatory alert management and inter-segment 
surveillance capabilities to facilitate proactive 
identification of potential market abuse. We continued 
to evaluate the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) to 
strengthen risk management and surveillance through 
advanced analytics and monitoring capabilities.

RISK MANAGEMENT
Risk is an inherent and inseparable part of any business 
environment. The Company recognises that, while risks 
cannot be entirely eliminated, they can be effectively 
identified, assessed, monitored and mitigated through 
a structured and proactive approach. Accordingly, risk 
management forms an integral part of the Company’s 
corporate governance and decision-making framework 
and is aimed at safeguarding long-term value creation, 
financial resilience and operational continuity.
The Company has in place a Board-approve

d Risk 
Management Policy, which provides the overarching 
framework for identification, assessment, monitoring and 
mitigation of internal and external risks. These include, inter 
alia, financial, operational, sectoral, technological, cyber 
security, regulatory, reputational, environmental and other 
emerging risks. The Policy also ensures that appropriate 
systems, controls, escalation mechanisms and reporting 
structures are established and maintained across the 
organisation. Further, business continuity planning and risk 
response strategies are embedded into both day-to-day 
operations and strategic business planning.
To strengthen risk governance, the Company has 
adopted a “Four Lines of Defence” model. The first line 
of defence comprises of the business and operational 
teams, supported by technology and process controls, 
who are responsible for managing and owning risks within 
their respective functions. The second line of defence 
consists of the risk management and compliance 
functions, which independently oversee risk exposures, 
monitor adherence to established frameworks and 
support effective implementation of controls. The third 
line of defence includes the internal audit, external audit 
and surveillance functions which periodically assess the 
adequacy and effectiveness of internal controls and 
identify areas requiring improvement. The fourth line of 
defence rests with the Risk Management Committee and 
Board of Directors, which provide strategic oversight and 
periodically review the adequacy and effectiveness of the 
Company’s risk management framework.
The Company follows an Enterprise Risk Management 
(“ERM”) approach to ensure continuous identification, 
categorisation, assessment and prioritisation of risks. This 
framework is supported by the use of Key Risk Indicators 
(“KRIs”) for ongoing monitoring and timely escalation of 
material risk exposures. Risk ownership is clearly defined 
and mitigation plans are periodically reviewed

to assess

overseeing the execution of its business objectives.

business plans and budgets; monitoring operational 
and financial performance; and overseeing significant 
investments, acquisitions, divestments, capital

Company’s governance framework and ensuring

practices.

internal control environment, including internal

compliance systems to ensure that material risks

evaluation, remuneration and succession planning

long-term objec

tives and Members interests.

Company’s financial reporting and disclosure 
processes and oversees the effectiveness of the 
independent audit function and compliance with 
applicable laws, regulations and standards.

Environmental, Social and Governance (‘ESG’) 
framework and Corporate Social Responsibility (‘CSR’) 
initiatives, ensuring that sustainability considerations 
are integrated into the Company’s strategy, risk 
management processes and business operations. It 
periodically reviews the Company’s ESG priorities, 
sustainability goals, performance and oversees 
initiatives relating to environmental stewardship, 
responsible business conduct, employee well-being, 
diversity and inclusion, community development and 
stakeholder engagement. The Board further ensures 
compliance with applicable ESG-related disclosure 
requirements and monitors the effectiveness and 
impact of CSR programmes undertaken by the 
Company in alignment with its commitment to 
sustainable and inclusive growth.
	
In addition, the Board periodically evaluates its own 
effectiveness, as well as that of its Committees and 
individual Directors, to strengthen governance and 
enhance Board performance. The Board fosters 
constructive engagement with Members and other 
stakeholders, promotes responsible and sustainable 
business practices and ensures that adequate 
Directors’ and Officers’ Liability Insurance coverage 
is maintained. It also ensures that Directors discharge 
their duties independently and objectively, free from 
any conflicts that may impair their judgment or

(c)	 Board Procedures
	
To facilitate effective planning and ensuring the 
availability of all Directors, the dates for Board 
Meetings for the ensuing financial year are scheduled 
well in advance. The proposed dates for the Meetings 
are then formally communicated to all Directors, 
enabling them to align their commitments and 
support meaningful participation in the Meetings.
	
The Board meets at least once a quarter to review the 
quarterly financial results and other agenda items. 
Additional Meetings are called, when necessary, to 
consider urgent business matters. There are minimum 
four Meetings of the Board in a financial year with a 
maximum gap of 120 days between two consecutive 
Meetings. In case of business exigencies or matter 
of urgency, resolutions are passed by circulation, 
as permitted by law and the same are noted at the 
subsequent Board Meeting.
	
All Committee recommendations placed before the 
Board during the year under review were unanimously 
accepted by the Board.
	
The quorum for the meeting of the Board is one-
third of the Board or three Directors, whichever is 
higher, including at least one Independent Director. 
During the year under review, the requisite quorum 
was present for all Board Meetings. Attendance 
at Board Meetings remained consistently strong, 
with participation well above the minimum quorum 
requirements for all Board Meetings.
	
The Board devotes its significant time in evaluation 
of current and potential strategic issues and reviews 
Company’s business plans, corporate strategy and 
risk manage

ment issues based on the markets it 
operates in and in light of the global industry trends 
and developments to help achieve its strategic goals.
	
In special and exceptional circumstances, 
consideration of additional or supplementary items 
are taken up with the approval of the Chairperson 
and majority of the Directors present in the Meeting, 
including one Independent Director.
	
Senior Management Personnel are invited to the 
Board/ Committee Meetings to provide additional 
inputs on the items being discussed by the Board/ 
Committees as and when necessary. The Managing 
Director and CEO apprises the Board on the overall 
performance of the Company, followed by the 
detailed presentation by the Chief Financial Officer 
and other Senior Executives of the Company.
	
The Meetings of the Board are generally held at the 
Registered Office of the Company. The Company 
offers the facility of video conferencing as prescribed 
under Section 173(2) of the Act read with Rule 3 of 
the Companies (Meetings of Board and its Powers) 
Rules, 2014, thereby saving resources and cost to the 
Company as well as the valued time of the Directors. 
The Board Meetings are either attended by the 
Directors in person or through video conferencing.
	
Availability of Information to the Board
	
The Board has access to all material information 
relating to the Company and its subsidiaries, including 
strategic priorities and business plans, the Annual 
Operating Plan, Financial Performance and Business 
Outlook, Budgets and Forecasts, Minutes of Meetings 
of the Board and its Committees, as well as those of 
the Boards of subsidiary companies. Board Meetings 
are governed by structured agenda.
	
The Board is furnished with timely, relevant and 
comprehensive information to facilitate informed 
decision-making and enable the effective discharge 
of its fiduciary, strategic and oversight responsibilities. 
The Board is also regularly apprised of material 
investments, acquisitions, stra

tegic partnerships 
and other significant business initiatives; if any, in 
financial obligations by or to the Company; significant 
litigation, regulatory actions; developments in 
technology, cybersecurity, human resources and 
other key operational areas; and compliance 
with applicable statutory, regulatory and listing 
requirements. Further, the Board receives periodic 
updates on risk management, governance matters, 
investor relations and stakeholder service-related 
issues, ensuring that it remains adequately informed 
of all material developments that may impact the 
Company’s operations, performance, reputation or 
long-term sustainability. The Board is periodically 
updated on regulatory changes, amendments and 
compliance obligations.
	
The detailed Agenda together with the relevant 
notes are circulated to the Board and Committee 
members in advance. All Agenda items are backed 
by background information as required to enable 
the Board to take informed decisions. The Company 
Secretary prepares the detailed Agenda for the 
Meetings, in consultation with the Senior Management 
and after approval of the Chairperson. Where prior 
circulation of any document is not practicable or 
where the Agenda item is of a confidential or sensitive 
nature, the relevant document is placed before the 
Board at the Meeting itself in line with authorization 
by the Board of Directors and Secretarial Standard-1 
on Meetings of the Board of Directors (‘SS-1’) issued 
by the Institute of Company Secretaries of India 
(‘ICSI’). Frequent and detailed deliberations on the 
agenda provide the strategic roadmap for the future 
growth of the Company.
	
Necessary information including but not limited 
to those mentioned in Part A of Schedule II of the 
Listing Regulations, are placed before the Board. 
The Directors are also provided on a quarterly basis, 
a compliance certificate which states that the 
Company has complied with all the applicable laws. 
This certificate is given

basis confirmation taken by 
the Company from each department confirming 
compliance with the laws applicable to their function. 
To strength the governance framework, all statutory 
policies are reviewed periodically by the Board.
	
For facilitating circulation of the agenda papers 
in electronic form and to reduce consumption of 
paper, the Company has adopted a web-based 
online software application for circulating Agendas, 
Minutes, Circular Resolutions and other papers 
relating to the Board/ Committee Meetings. The 
Board and Committee members of the Company 
receive the agenda papers in electronic form through 
this software application, which can be accessed 
only through ios/web with their respective login 
credentials. The application meets the high standards 
of security and integrity required for circulation 
and storage of the Board/ Committee Agenda and 
Minutes in electronic form. The online portal helps the 
Board and Committee members to access to Meeting 
materials, Agenda and Minutes on a real time basis 
while maintaining transparency and confidentiality.
	
During the Board/ Committee Meetings the Board 
members express their views on the items presented 
for discussion and make valuable suggestions as 
required to overcome challenges, always considering 
the best interest of the Company and its stakeholders.
	
Minutes of the Meetings
	
In compliance with the applicable Secretarial 
Standards issued by the ICSI, the draft Minutes of 
the Meetings are circulated amongst the Members 
of the Board and Committees. Comments and 
suggestions, if any, received from the Directors/
Committee Members are incorporated in the 
Minutes, in consultation with the Chairperson of the 
Board and Committees. Thereafter, signed Minutes of 
the Meetings are circulated amongst the Board and 
Committee Members.
	
Post Meeting follow-up mechanism
	
The important decisions taken at the Board 
/ Committee meetings are communicated to 
concerned departments promptly.

The Company 
has an effective post Meeting follow-up review 
and reporting mechanism for the decisions 
taken/suggestions provided by the Board and 
the Committees. The important decisions taken/
suggestions provided at the Board / Committee 
Meetings, which call for actions to be taken, are well 
documented  and wherever required, communicated 
to the concerned departments for their further action. 
The action taken report is placed at the immediately 
succeeding Meeting of the Board / Committees for 
information and review by the Board/ Committees.

Auditor and the Statutory Auditor, in carrying

external expertise, if required. The management 
is responsible for the preparation, presentation

The Company has established a robust internal 
audit and assurance framework to support 
effective risk management, governance 
and internal control processes. An Internal 
Audit Policy and Charter approved by the 
Board provides the overall framework for the 
functioning of the Internal Audit function and 
defines its roles, responsibilities, authority and 
operating methodology. The Policy also set

s out 
the approach for preparation of the Risk-Based 
Internal Audit (‘RBIA’) Plan and the risk-based 
rating methodology for audit observations, 
thereby ensuring a structured and consistent 
assessment of risks and controls across the 
organisation.

RBIA Plan annually, which is developed in line 
with applicable regulatory requirements and 
leading governance practices. The plan is based 
on an independent and comprehensive risk 
assessment covering the Company’s businesses,

assurance on the adequacy and effectiveness

Complaints Redress Platform (SCORES):

complaints and track the status of redressal online 
on the website at https://scores.sebi.gov.in/. It 
also enables the market intermediaries and listed 
companies to receive the complaints from investors 
against them, redress such complaints and report 
redressal of such complaints. All the activities starting 
from lodging of a complaint till its disposal are carried 
online in an automated environment and the status 
of every complaint can be viewed online at any 
time. The Company has registered itself on SCORES 
and endeavours to resolve all investor complaints 
received through SCORES expeditiously.

guidelines for Members to resolve their grievances

A brief on types of customers
	
	
Nuvama is a leading integrated wealth management company in India, serving ultra-high-net-worth families, 
high-net-worth and affluent individuals, family offices, corporates, and institutions. The diversified scaled 
platform spans Wealth Management, Asset Management, Asset Services, and Capital Markets, providing 
comprehensive solutions to meet the evolving needs of our clients.
	
	
The Company’s clientele is distributed across the following business verticals:
	
	
• 	
Wealth Management
	
	
	
Nuvama Private (Ultra-High-Net-Worth Clients):
 
 
 
This segment serves more than 4750+ families, including entrepreneurs, business owners, family offices, 
CXOs, professional investors, and institutions.
	
	
	
Nuvama Wealth (Affluent and High-Net-Worth Clients):
	
	
	
With a client base exceeding 1.3 million, this segment primarily caters to salaried professionals and owners 
of small and medium-sized enterprises.
	
	
• 	
Nuvama Asset Management
 
 
 
The asset management division serves institutions, family offices, UHNIs, and HNIs. Products are dist

ributed 
through both internal channels, such as Nuvama Private and Nuvama Wealth, and external distribution 
partners.
	
	
• 	
Nuvama Asset Services
	
	
	
The Asset Services business delivers clearing and custody solutions to over 275 clients, including domestic 
and international institutional investors. Internationally, the Company serves foreign portfolio investors, 
while domestically, its clientele mainly includes alternate investment funds and portfolio managers.
	
	
• 	
Nuvama Capital Markets
 
 
 
The capital markets division comprises institutional equities and investment banking services. It supports 
more than 900 corporates and institutions, providing comprehensive financial solutions backed by deep 
market expertise.
	
	
	
Overall, Nuvama serves a wide spectrum of clients across multiple business segments, demonstrating 
its commitment to delivering personalized financial solutions and exceptional service across its diverse 
range of offerings. Additional details can be found in the Company’s business overview section.

we remain committed to environmental stewardship and responsible business 
growth through collaboration with our employees, partners, and communities.
As we move forward, we will continue to strengthen our sustainability practices, 
enhance transparency, and pursue continuous improvement in creating long-term 
value for all stakeholders. We thank our employees, customers, investors, partners,

PRINCIPLE 3: Businesses should respect and promote the well-being of all employees, including 
those in their value chains.
(This principle emphasizes the importance of employee well-being. Companies should provide safe and healthy working 
conditions, fair wages, and opportunities for career development to all employees in their value chains, including suppliers, 
contractors, and temporary workers.)
Essential Indicators
1 	
a. 	 Details of measures for the well-being of employees:
 
 
At Nuvama, employee well-being is a key priority. We offer a comprehensive suite of benefits designed to 
suppo

rt the physical, mental well-being of our workforce. All permanent employees are covered under health 
insurance, term life insurance, and personal accident insurance programs. The Company’s Mediclaim program 
supports diverse healthcare needs through coverage for advanced treatments, IVF and fertility treatments, 
gender reassignment procedures, and other modern medical interventions, subject to policy terms and 
conditions.
	
	
Recognizing the evolving healthcare needs of employees and their families, the Company also provides 
employees with the option of additional top-up health insurance plans, enabling enhanced coverage and 
greater financial protection against rising healthcare costs.
	
	
In addition, we offer a range of employee support initiatives, including personal loan assistance, Happiness 
Leave, maternity and parental benefits, health counselling services, and annual health check-ups, ensuring 
holistic support across different life stages.
 
 
To further support women employees during motherhood, Nuvama extends benefits beyond statutory maternity 
leave. Employees are provided with additional Care Leave prior to the commencement of maternity leave to 
support their health and well-being during pregnancy. We also provide travel assistance support to ensure 
safe and comfortable commuting during this period.
	
	
As part of our employee welfare initiatives, retiring employees and their eligible family members continue to 
remain covered under the Group Mediclaim Policy and Group Term Life Insurance Policy until the expiry of the 
applicable policy period for that financial year.
 
 
Recognizing the importance of flexibility and work-life integration, Nuvama enables employees to avail work-
from-home arrangements on an exception basis, subject to business requirements and role suitability. Such 
arrangements may be considered in cases including maternity, post-medical recovery, family caregiving 
responsibilities, or personal emergencies.
	
	
To dr

ive meaningful POSH awareness through our Ethics Line platform, the Company complements traditional 
training methods with engaging initiatives such as Nukkad Natak (street plays). These interactive sessions 
help employees understand POSH principles through relatable scenarios, encouraging greater awareness and 
practical application.
	
	
At Nuvama, we believe that listening is the foundation of trust, engagement, and growth. Through formal listening 
platforms, leadership interactions, feedback forums, surveys, and confidential channels, we provide employees 
with multiple avenues to share ideas, feedback, and concerns. Insights gathered through these channels help 
shape employee experience initiatives and strengthen our people practices.
	
	
At Nuvama, recognition is embedded in our culture. Through APPLAUD, our digital recognition platform, and 
Kudos, our spot recognition program, complemented by bi-annual and annual awards, we celebrate employee 
contributions and achievements across the organization.
 
 
Well-being at Nuvama extends beyond traditional benefits. Through Nuvama Cares, we provide a holistic well-
being ecosystem that supports employees and their families across physical, emotional, and social wellness. 
The program offers access to healthcare, preventive care, mental wellness, fitness solutions, and family-
focused support initiatives.

The Company adopts a proactive approach to ensuring operational resilience and uninterrupted business continuity.

prevent the unauthorized transfer of sensitive information, including personally identifiable information (PII). Regular 
vulnerability assessments are conducted to identify and mitigate potential security risks across the organization. 
In addition to data encryption, network firewalls and web application firewalls have been deployed to enhance 
protection against cyber threats.
	
The Company has also established privileged access monitoring mechanisms to control and oversee access to 
critical systems and information. A dedicated Security Operations Center (SOC) continuously monitors security 
events and incidents, enabling timely detection and response. Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) solutions 
have been implemented to monitor and mitigate risks associated with endpoint devices. To further strengthen 
cybersecurity awareness, the Information Security team regularly conducts phishing simulations, cyber awareness 
quizzes, and employee engagement initiatives, including awareness emails and informational posters.

and off-site storage solutions. Additionally, a comprehensive Business Continuity Policy has been developed based

significant changes occur.

separate seismic zone. Regular drills and testing exercises are conducted to assess readiness and ensure the 
organization’s ability to respond effectively to potential disruptions.

Report on the Internal Financial Controls 
under Clause (i) of Sub-section 3 of 
Section 143 of the Companies Act, 2013 
(“the Act”)
In conjunction with our audit of the consolidated financial 
statements of Nuvama Wealth Management Limited 
(hereinafter referred to as the “Holding Company”) as of 
and for the year ended March 31, 2026, we have audited the 
internal financial controls with reference to consolidated 
financial statements of the Holding Company and its 
subsidiaries (the Holding Company and its subsidiaries 
together referred to as “the Group”) , its associate and 
joint venture, which are companies incorporated in India, 
as of that date.
Management’s Responsibility for Internal 
Financial Controls
The respective Board of Directors of the companies 
included in the Group, its associate and joint venture, 
which are companies incorporated in India, are responsible 
for establishing and maintaining internal financial controls 
based on the internal control over financial reporting 
criteria established by the Holding Company considering 
the essential components of internal control stated in the 
Guidance Note on Audit of Internal Financial Controls Over 
Financial Reporting issued by the Institute of Chartered 
Accountants of India (ICAI). These responsibilities 
include the design, implementation and maintenance of 
adequate internal financial controls that were operating 
effectively for ensuring the orderly and efficient conduct 
of its business, including adherence to the respective 
company’s policies, the safeguarding of its assets, the 
prevention and detection of frauds and errors, the 
accuracy and completeness of the accounting records, 
and the timely preparation of reliable financial information, 
as required under the Companies Act, 2013.
Auditor’s Responsibility
Our responsibility is to express an opinion on the Holding 
Company’s internal financial controls with reference to 
consolid

ated financial statements based on our audit. 
We conducted our audit in accordance with the Guidance 
Note on Audit of Internal Financial Controls Over Financial 
Reporting (the “Guidance Note”) and the Standards on 
Auditing, specified under section 143(10) of the Act, to 
the extent applicable to an audit of internal financial 
controls, both, issued by ICAI. Those Standards and 
the Guidance Note require that we comply with ethical 
requirements and plan and perform the audit to obtain 
reasonable assurance about whether adequate internal 
financial controls with reference to consolidated financial 
statements was established and maintained and if such 
controls operated effectively in all material respects.
Our audit involves performing procedures to obtain 
audit evidence about the adequacy of the internal 
financial controls with reference to consolidated financial 
statements and their operating effectiveness. Our audit of 
internal financial controls with reference to consolidated 
financial statements included obtaining an understanding 
of internal financial controls with reference to consolidated 
financial statements, assessing the risk that a material 
weakness exists, and testing and evaluating the design 
and operating effectiveness of internal control based on 
the assessed risk. The procedures selected depend on 
the auditor’s judgement, including the assessment of the 
risks of material misstatement of the financial statements, 
whether due to fraud or error.
We believe that the audit evidence we have obtained and 
the audit evidence obtained by the other auditors in terms 
of their reports referred to in the Other Matters paragraph 
below, is sufficient and appropriate to provide a basis for 
our audit opinion on the internal financial controls with 
reference to consolidated financial statements.
Meaning of Internal Financial Controls 
with Reference to Consolidated Financial 
Statements
A company’s internal financial control with reference to

consolidated financial statements is a process designed 
to provide reasonable assurance regarding the reliability 
of financial reporting and the preparation of financial 
statements for external purposes in accordance with 
generally accepted accounting principles. A company’s 
internal financial control with reference to consolidated 
financial statements includes those policies and 
procedures that (1) pertain to the maintenance of 
records that, in reasonable detail, accurately and fairly 
reflect the transactions and dispositions of the assets 
of the company; (2) provide reasonable assurance 
that transactions are recorded as necessary to permit 
preparation of financial statements in accordance with 
generally accepted accounting principles, and that 
receipts and expenditures of the company are being made 
only in accordance with authorisations of management 
and directors of the company; and (3) provide reasonable 
assurance regarding prevention or timely detection 
of unauthorised acquisition, use, or disposition of the 
company’s assets that could have a material effect on the 
financial statements.
Inherent Limitations of Internal Financial 
Controls with Reference to Consolidated 
Financial Statements
Because of the inherent limitations of internal financial 
controls with reference to consolidated financial 
statements, including the possibility of collusion or 
improper management override of controls, material 
misstatements due to error or fraud may occur and not be 
detected. Also, projections of any evaluation of the internal 
financial controls with reference to consolidated financial 
statements to future periods are subject to the risk that the 
internal financial controls with reference to consolidated 
financial statements may become inadequate because of 
changes in conditions, or that the degree of compliance 
with the policies or procedures may deteriorate.
Opinion
In our opinion, the Group , its associate and joint venture, 
which are co

mpanies incorporated in India, have, 
maintained in all material respects, adequate internal 
financial controls with reference to consolidated financial 
statements and such internal financial controls with 
reference to consolidated financial statements were 
operating effectively as at March 31, 2026, based on the 
internal control over financial reporting criteria established 
by the Holding Company considering the essential 
components of internal control stated in the Guidance 
Note issued by the ICAI.
Other Matters
Our report under Section 143(3)(i) of the Act on the 
adequacy and operating effectiveness of the internal 
financial controls with reference to consolidated financial 
statements of the Holding Company, in so far as it relates 
to these eight subsidiaries, one associate and one joint 
venture, which are companies incorporated in India, is 
based on the corresponding reports of the auditors of such 
subsidiaries, associate and joint venture incorporated in 
India.

2. 	 Basis of preparation of consolidated 
financial statements
	
The consolidated financial statements relate to 
Nuvama Wealth Management Limited (‘the Company’) 
and its subsidiaries (together ‘the Group’), associate 
and joint venture.
	
The consolidated financial statements have been 
prepared in accordance with Indian Accounting 
Standards (Ind AS) notified under the Companies 
(Indian Accounting Standards) Rules, 2015 (as 
amended from time to time). These consolidated 
financial statements have been approved for issue 
by the Board of Directors of the Company on May 11, 
2026.
	
These consolidated financial statements have been 
prepared on a historical cost basis, except for certain 
financial instruments such as derivative financial 
instruments and other financial instruments held 
for trading, which have been measured at a lower 
of carrying value and fair value and assets classified 
as held for sale, which have been measured at fair 
value less cost to sell. The consolidated financial 
statements are presented in Indian Rupees (Rs.), all 
values are rounded to the nearest crore and rounded 
off to two decimal places, except when otherwise 
indicated. Accordingly, amounts less than Rs. 0.01 
crore are shown as Rs. 0.00 crore.
3.	 Presentation of consolidated financial 
statements
	
The Group prepares and presents its Balance Sheet, 
Statement of Profit and Loss and Statement of 
Changed in Equity in the format prescribed in the 
Division III of the Schedule III to the Companies 
Act, 2013. The Statement of Cash Flows has been 
prepared and presented as per the requirements of 
IND AS. An analysis regarding recovery or

settlement 
within 12 months after the reporting date (current) 
and more than 12 months after the reporting date 
(non–current) is presented in note 45.
	
Financial assets and financial liabilities are generally 
reported gross in the balance sheet. They are only 
offset and reported net when, in addition to having an 
unconditional legally enforceable right to offset the 
recognised amounts without being contingent on a 
future event, the parties also intend to settle on a net 
basis in all of the following circumstances:
	
•	
The normal course of business
	
•	
The event of default
	
•	
The event of insolvency or bankruptcy of the 
Group and/or its counterparties
4.	 Basis of consolidation:
	
The consolidated financial statements comprise 
the financial statements of the Company and its 
subsidiaries. The Company consolidates a subsidiary 
when it controls it. Control is achieved when the 
Group is exposed, or has rights, to variable returns 
from its involvement with the investee and has the 
ability to affect those returns through its power 
over the investee. Generally, there is a presumption 
that a majority of voting rights result in control. To 
support this presumption and when the Group has 
less than a majority of the voting or similar rights of 
an investee, the Group considers all relevant facts 
and circumstances in assessing whether it has power 
over an investee, including:
	
•	
The contractual arrangement with the other vote 
holders of the investee
	
•	
Rights arising from other contractual 
arrangements

Consolidated financial statements are prepared using

However, no subsidiaries, associate and joint venture 
have followed different accounting policies than

The financial statements of all entities used for the

Consolidation procedure:
	
a.	
Combine like items of assets, liabilities, equity, 
income, expenses and cash flows of the parent 
with those of its subsidiaries. For this purpose, 
income and expenses of the subsidiary are 
based on the amounts of the assets and 
liabilities recognised in the consolidated 
financ

ial statements at the acquisition date.
	
b.	
Offset (eliminate) the carrying amount of the 
parent’s investment in each subsidiary and the 
parent’s portion of equity of each subsidiary.
	
c.	
Eliminate in full intragroup assets and liabilities, 
equity, income, expenses and cash flows relating 
to transactions between entities of the Group 
(profits or losses resulting from intragroup 
transactions that are recognised in assets, 
are eliminated in full). Income Taxes applies 
to temporary differences that arise from the 
elimination of profits and losses resulting from 
intragroup transactions.
	
Profit or loss and each component of OCI are 
attributed to the equity holders of the parent of the 
Group and to the non-controlling interests, even if 
this results in the non-controlling interests having a 
deficit balance.
	
All intra-group assets, liabilities, equity, income, 
expenses and cash flows relating to transactions 
between members of the Group are eliminated in full 
on consolidation.
	
Disclosures for investment interest in other entities 
are provided in Note 52.
	
The financial statements of all subsidiaries 
incorporated outside India are converted on the 
following basis: (a) Income and expenses are 
converted at the rate of exchange on the date on 
which transaction first qualifies for recognition 
and (b) All assets and liabilities are translated at 
the closing rate as on the Balance Sheet date. The 
exchange difference arising out of period/year 
end translation is debited or credited as “Foreign 
Exchange Translation Reserve” forming part of Other 
Comprehensive Income and accumulated as a 
separate component of other equity.
	
Investment in associates and joint venture:
	
An associate is an entity over which the Group has 
significant influence. Significant influence is the 
power to participate in the financial and operating 
policy decision of the investee, but is not control or 
joint control of those policies.
	
A joint venture is an

entity in which the Group has the 
ability to exercise control jointly. In a joint venture, 
parties have proportionate interests in the assets and 
liabilities of the joint venture entity.
	
The considerations made in determining whether 
significant influence are similar to those necessary 
to determine control over the subsidiaries.
•
	
The Group’s investment in its associate / joint venture 
is accounted for using the equity method. Under the 
equity method, the investment in an associate / joint 
venture is initially recognised at cost. The carrying 
amount of the investment is adjusted to recognise 
changes in the Group’s share of net assets of the 
associate since the acquisition date.
	
The statement of profit and loss reflects the Group’s 
share of the results of operations of the associate 
/ joint venture. Any change in other comprehensive 
income (OCI) of those investees is presented as a 
part of the Group’s other comprehensive income 
(OCI).
	
The financial statements of the associate / joint 
venture are prepared for the same reporting period 
as the Group. When necessary, adjustments are 
made to bring the accounting policies in line with 
those of the Group.
	
After application of the equity method, the Group 
determines whether it is necessary to recognise an 
impairment loss on its investment in its associate 
/ joint venture. At each reporting date, the Group 
determines whether there is objective evidence 
that the investment in the associate / joint venture 
is impaired. If there is such evidence, the Group 
calculates the amount of impairment as the 
difference between the recoverable amount of the 
associate / joint venture and its carrying value and 
then recognises the loss in the statement of profit 
and loss.
5.	 Material accounting policy 
information
5.1	 Revenue from contract with customer
	
Revenue is measured at transaction price i.e. the 
amount of consideration to which the Group expects 
to be entitled in exchange for tran

sferring promised 
goods or services to the customer, excluding 
amounts collected on behalf of third parties. The 
Group consider the terms of the contracts and its 
customary business practices to determine the 
transaction price. Where the consideration promised 
is variable, the Group excludes the estimates of 
variable consideration that are constrained. The 
Group applies the five-step approach for recognition 
of revenue:
	
i.	
Identification of contract(s) with customers;
	
ii.	
Identification of the separate performance 
obligations in the contract;
	
iii.	
Determination of transaction price;
	
iv.	
Allocation of transaction price to the separate 
performance obligations; and
	
v.	
Recognition of revenue when (or as) each 
performance obligation is satisfied
	
The group recognises revenue from the following 
sources:
	
a.	
Brokerage income including client subscription 
fees is recognised as per contracted rates at the 
point in time when transaction’s performance 
obligation is satisfied on behalf of the customers 
on the trade date.s
	
b.	
Fee income including merchant banking, advisory 
fees, distribution services and commissions, 
fund accounting fees etc is accounted on an 
accrual basis as per Ind AS 115 and in accordance 
with the terms and contracts entered with the 
client.
	
c.	
Clearing fees income arises, when the 
performance obligation related to the trade is 
executed and a valid contract is generated for 
the trade.
	
d.	
Research services fee income and Interest on 
delayed payments is accounted when there is 
reasonable certainty as to its receipts.
	
e.	
Asset management fees is recognised in 
accordance with the Investment management 
agreement.
	
f.	
Portfolio management fees is recognised over the 
tenure in accordance with portfolio management 
agreement entered with respective clients.
	
g.	
Rental income is accounted on a straight-line 
basis over the lease terms on operating leases.

 Under Ind AS 109 interest income is recorded 
using the effective interest rate (EIR) method for all 
financial instruments measured at amortised cost 
and debt instrument measured at FVOCI. The EIR 
is the rate that exactly discounts estimated future 
cash flows through the expected life of the financial

 The EIR is calculated by taking into account any 
discount or premium on acquisition, fees and 
costs that are an integral part of the EIR. The Group 
recognises interest income using a rate of return 
that represents the best estimate of a constant 
rate of return over the expected life of the financial 
asset. Hence, it recognises the effect of potentially 
different interest rates charged at various stages, 
and other characteristics of the product life cycle 
including prepayments penalty interest and charges.
	
 If expectations regarding the cash flows on the 
financial asset are revised for reasons other than 
credit risk, the adjustment is booked as a positive 
or negative adjustment to the carrying amount of 
the asset in the balance sheet with an increase or 
reduction in interest income.
	
 The Group calculates interest income by applying 
the EIR to the gross carrying amount of financial 
assets other than credit-impaired assets.
	
 When a financial asset becomes credit-impaired 
and is, therefore, regarded as ‘Stage 3’, the Group 
calculates interest income by applying the EIR to 
the amortised cost (net of expected credit

loss) of 
the financial asset. If the financial asset cures and 
is no longer credit-impaired, the Group reverts to 
calculating interest income on a gross basis.
5.2.2 Dividend income:
	
Dividend income is recognised when the right to 
receive payment is established, it is probable that 
the economic benefits associated with the dividend 
will flow to the entity and the amount of the dividend 
can be measured reliably.

5.3.1 Date of recognition
	
Financial assets and financial liabilities with exception

5.4 Financial assets and liabilities
5.4.1 Amortized cost and effective interest rate (EIR)
	
The effective interest rate is a method of calculating 
the amortised cost of a debt instrument and of 
allocating interest income over the relevant period.
	
For financial instruments other than purchased 
or originated credit-impaired financial assets, the 
effective interest rate is the rate that exactly discounts 
estimated future cash receipts (including all fees and 
points paid or received that form an integral part of 
the effective interest rate, transaction costs and 
other premiums or discounts) excluding expected 
credit losses, through the expected life of the debt

instrument, or, where appropriate, a shorter period, 
to the gross carrying amount of the debt instrument 
on initial recognition. For purchased or originated 
credit impaired financial assets, a credit-adjusted 
effective interest rate is calculated by discounting 
the estimated future cash flows, including expected 
credit losses, to the amortised cost of the debt 
instrument on initial recognition.
	
The amortised cost of a financial asset is the amount 
at which the financial asset is measured at initial 
recognition minus the principal repayments, plus 
the cumulative amortisation using the effective 
interest method of any difference between that 
initial amount and the maturity amount, adjusted 
for any loss allowance. On the other hand, the gross 
carrying amount of a financial asset is the amortised 
cost of a financial asset before adjusting for any loss 
allowance.
5.4.2 Financial assets held for trading

Embedded derivatives
	
An embedded derivative is a component of a hybrid

contract with the effect that some of the cash flows

to stand-alone derivative. An embedded derivative 
causes some or all of the cash flows that otherwise

of a non-financial variable, it is not specific to a party 
to the contract.

accounted for as separate derivatives and recorded 
at fair value if their economic characteristics and risks 
are not closely related to those of the host contracts 
and the host contracts are not held for trading or 
designated at fai

embedded derivatives are measured at fair value 
with changes in fair value recognised in profit or loss, 
unless designated as effective hedging instruments.

5.6 Derecognition of financial Instruments
5.6.1 Derecognition of financial asset
	
A financial asset (or, where applicable a part of a 
financial asset or a part of a group of similar financial 
assets) is derecognised when the rights to receive 
cash flows from the financial asset have expired. The 
Group also derecognises the financial asset if it has 
both transferred the financial asset and the transfer 
qualifies for derecognition.
	
The Group has transferred the financial asset if, and 
only if, either
	
•	
The Group has transferred the rights to receive 
cash flows from the financial asset or
	
•	
It retains the contractual rights to receive the 
cash flows of the financial asset, but assumed a 
contractual obligation to pay the cash flows in 
full without material delay to third party under 
pass through arrangement.
	
Pass-through arrangements are transactions 
whereby the Group retains the contractual rights 
to receive the cash flows of a financial asset (the 
‘original asset’), but assumes a contractual obligation 
to pay those cash flows to one or more entities (the 
‘eventual recipients’), when all of the following three 
conditions are met:
	
•	
The Group has no obligation to pay amounts to 
the eventual recipients unless it has collected 
equivalent amounts from the original asset, 
excluding short-term advances with the right 
to full recovery of the amount lent plus accrued 
interest at market rates.
	
•	
The Group cannot sell or pledge the original 
asset other than as security to the eventual 
recipients
	
•	
The Group has to remit any cash flows it collects 
on behalf of the eventual recipients without 
material delay. In addition, the Group is not 
entitled to reinvest such cash flows, except 
for investments in cash or cash equivalents 
including interest earned, during the period 
between the collection date and the date of 
required remittance to the even

tual recipients.
	
A transfer only qualifies for derecognition if either:
	
•	
The Group has transferred substantially all the 
risks and rewards of the asset; or
	
•	
The Group has neither transferred nor retained 
substantially all the risks and rewards of the 
asset, but has transferred control of the asset.
	
The Group considers control to be transferred if 
and only if, the transferee has the practical ability 
to sell the asset in its entirety to an unrelated third 
party and is able to exercise that ability unilaterally 
and without imposing additional restrictions on the 
transfer.
5.6.2 Derecognition of financial liabilities
	
A financial liability is derecognised when the obligation 
under the liability is discharged, cancelled or expires. 
Where an existing financial liability is replaced by 
another from the same lender on substantially 
different terms, or the terms of an existing liability 
are substantially modified, such an exchange or 
modification is treated as a derecognition of the 
original liability and the recognition of a new liability. 
The difference between the carrying value of the 
original financial liability and the consideration paid 
is recognised in the statement profit or loss.
